Does the candidate hold NBPTS certification?
If not NBPTS, did the candidate complete an EPP recognized by the Ontario authority, and does the candidate hold a passing score on an out-of-state exam for elementary?
Which exam (name and score) did the candidate pass, and is it the Ontario-recognized exam for the license area?
What is the candidate's highest degree level and the EPP completed for it?
Are the 5 years of experience licensed teaching experience (not unlicensed or non-teaching)?
Has the candidate ever held a North Carolina license before?
not_covered: Ontario's own licensing requirements, the content of its certificate, and whether it is 'renewable' under Ontario law. The policies do not describe Ontario's system.
Whether the candidate's foreign teaching experience counts toward NC salary experience credit. LICN-006 addresses NC school unit experience and does not address foreign teaching experience.
The Beginning Teacher Support Program requirements in TCED-016, which the policies reference but do not include.
The NC testing requirements that apply to a CPL route for elementary, since LICN-025 §1(b)'s elementary exam rule addresses the IPL route only.
Any separate fee for an out-of-state CPL application.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line: five years exceeds the three-year IPL limit, so the CPL route under LICN-025 applies, and the candidate's status on the clear-license and NBPTS/substantially-similar criteria must be confirmed. Its claims are well cited, with minor gaps in the LICN-024 §1 description and the elementary testing discussion, and it omits the BTSP and Elementary-test uncertainty points only partly.

question: Applicant with a BS in engineering, 4 years in industry, wants to teach physics in NC. Is there a non-traditional path?

answer.summary: Yes, the policies provide several routes for a bachelor's-degree holder without an education degree: a Permit to Teach, an Emergency License, or a Residency License, each requested by the hiring school unit. Which one applies depends on the applicant's physics coursework hours, whether they have passed the Praxis physics test (5266, score 145), and whether they have ever held a North Carolina educator license.

claims.text: A Permit to Teach may be requested by a public school unit's governing body for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license. The applicant's BS meets the degree requirement, but eligibility also depends on having no prior NC educator license.
A Permit to Teach is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed.
For State Salary Schedule pay, a Permit to Teach is issued at the bachelor's-degree (A-Level) zero-years-of-experience level regardless of education level or prior work experience.

An Emergency License may be requested by a public school unit for an applicant who holds a bachelor's degree that includes at least 18 credit hours of coursework relevant to the licensure area, has not completed a recognized educator preparation program in that area, and does not qualify for a residency license. Physics coursework from the engineering degree would need to count as relevant coursework for this route.
An Emergency License is a one-year nonrenewable license and cannot be extended or renewed.
An Emergency License holder is paid at the A-Level zero-experience rate for the State Salary Schedule but may qualify for graduate degree pay or experience pay under LICN-006.

A Residency License may be requested by a public school unit for an applicant who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination for that content area.
The North Carolina licensure exam for Secondary Physics (license code 320) is Praxis test 5266 with a required score of 145.

A Residency License is a one-year license, renewable twice. To renew, the employing PSU must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program, is employed as a teacher, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year.

A PSU employing a teacher on a Residency License must provide at least three hours of field experience before classroom teaching and at least 10 hours over the first year, plus 10 days of professional development.

Non-teaching work experience can earn one year of experience credit for each year of full-time relevant work completed after the bachelor's degree. Four years of qualifying work would equal four years of experience credit (4 ÷ 1 = 4). The work must be at least half-time (20+ hours per week), completed after age 18, not on-the-job training, paid and documented, and must be recommended by the PSU and found by DPI to be directly related to the license area (physics).
Non-teaching experience credit is not transferable to licensure areas for which the experience is not relevant, so credit depends on the physics relevance of the engineering work.

questions_for_user: How many semester credit hours of physics coursework does the applicant have, and does any of the engineering coursework count as physics coursework?
Has the applicant passed the Praxis physics test (5266) with a score of at least 145?
Has the applicant ever been issued any North Carolina professional educator license?
Will a North Carolina public school unit employ the applicant and agree to request the license?
Is the applicant willing to enroll in a recognized educator preparation program, which is required to renew a Residency License?
Does the applicant intend to teach for one year or longer? Permit and Emergency licenses expire at the end of the fiscal year or after one year and cannot be renewed.
not_covered: Whether engineering coursework counts as relevant or physics coursework for the 18-hour and 24-hour thresholds. The policies do not define relevance for those thresholds.
The text of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which sets the underlying eligibility requirement for Emergency and Residency licenses and is not included in the passages.
What the term non-traditional path means. The policies do not use it, so this answer identifies the permit, emergency, and residency routes.
Which educator preparation programs are recognized and what alternative-route program requirements apply.

Any other route for a bachelor's-degree holder beyond the Permit, Emergency, and Residency licenses, such as an initial professional license, which requires completion of an educator preparation program in North Carolina or outside it.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly identifies the permit, emergency, and residency routes and cites accurate policy text for its claims. It never states that industry experience is not a licensure qualification, omits the default EPP route, the eight-hour training requirement for non-EPP hires, and the out-of-state IPL experience point, and does not flag that G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) is missing from the corpus.

question: Candidate has a PhD in curriculum and instruction, no K-12 classroom time, wants to be an admin. Eligible?

answer.summary: A PhD does not by itself make the candidate eligible. Eligibility depends on whether the PhD was completed through a State Board-approved administrator preparation program (APP) and on which administrator role the candidate wants. The provided policies do not require K-12 classroom teaching for an administrator license.

claims.text: To qualify for an administrator license, an applicant must meet G.S. 115C-270.20(b)(1) and other requirements in LICN-011. The statute itself is not among the provided passages, so its content is unknown.

For any administrator license other than superintendent or Exceptional Children program administrator, the applicant must have completed an administrator preparation program at the master's (M), specialist (S), or doctoral (D) level.

An APP is a program approved by the State Board of Education to prepare, train, and recommend candidates for administrator licensure. A PhD in curriculum and instruction counts toward the APP requirement only if it was completed through such an approved program. The policies provided do not say whether a curriculum and instruction doctorate qualifies on its own.

For a principal license, the master's degree must be in School Administration, Educational Leadership, or another education-related field. The provided policies do not say how a doctorate in a different field is treated for this requirement.
An applicant is eligible only at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP or APP. If the PhD was completed through an APP, it would be the relevant level (D-level).

Superintendent licensure requires an administrator preparation program at the specialist or doctoral level, plus either a principal license and superintendent license, or a bachelor's degree and five years of relevant leadership or managerial experience deemed relevant by the hiring local board.

The administrator license provisions provided (LICN-011) list no K-12 classroom teaching requirement. Assistant principal employment requires either a principal license or a provisional assistant principal license under LICN-014 Section 7, which is not among the provided passages.

An applicant must satisfy any applicable licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, and must attempt them at least once during the first year. If the exam is not satisfied before initial application, the applicant receives an initial professional license rather than a continuing professional license. The principal exam is the North Carolina Principal Portfolio Assessment, which must be completed with a validated score.

questions_for_user: Which administrator role does the candidate want (principal, assistant principal, superintendent, curriculum-instructional specialist, Exceptional Children program administrator, or other)?
Was the PhD completed through a State Board-approved administrator preparation program (APP), or through a different doctoral program?

Is the PhD in curriculum and instruction the only graduate degree? If the candidate wants a principal license, does the candidate also hold a master's in School Administration, Educational Leadership, or a related education field?
Has the candidate completed or attempted the required licensure exam (for a principal, the NC Principal Portfolio Assessment)? When was the first attempt, or when was the first year of licensure?
Does the candidate hold any current North Carolina or out-of-state educator license, and if so, which type?
Is the candidate seeking a North Carolina license for an assistant principal position, which requires a principal license or a provisional assistant principal license under LICN-014 Section 7?
premise_corrections: The question treats the lack of K-12 classroom time as a barrier. The administrator license provisions provided do not require classroom teaching. The governing factors are APP completion, degree level, role, and exam status. Classroom time could matter only under requirements not included in the passages (for example, LICN-014 or the statute).
not_covered: The content of G.S. 115C-270.20(b)(1), which LICN-011 incorporates by reference.
The content of LICN-014 Section 7 (provisional assistant principal license), which governs assistant principal eligibility.
Whether a curriculum and instruction PhD from a non-APP program can satisfy administrator licensure in any form.
Experience requirements for principal licensure (the passages give experience only for superintendents).
Details of the NC Principal Portfolio Assessment beyond the table entry.
Pre-2026 rules that may have applied to this candidate's earlier coursework or degree.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly identifies that classroom experience is not required, that APP completion and degree level govern eligibility, and that the principal, superintendent, and assistant principal rules are accurately cited. It omits the curriculum-instructional specialist exam (test 5412, score 146), which is the most relevant licensure exam for a C&I PhD holder, and says nothing about salary experience credit, though the latter does not affect licensure.

question: Teacher on an Initial Professional License in art, wants to move to CPL. Has 2 years of experience. Can they upgrade now?

answer.summary: Not yet. A teacher on an Initial Professional License must have at least three years of licensed teaching experience before converting to a Continuing Professional License, so two years does not qualify. The teacher can convert once they reach three years of licensed teaching experience and meet the other conditions, including the art exam requirement and the Beginning Teacher Support Program.

claims.text: To qualify for a continuing professional teacher license, an applicant must hold an NC initial professional license or residency license, satisfy the licensure examination requirements, have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and have completed a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.
With two years of experience, the teacher does not meet the three-year licensed teaching experience requirement, so the teacher cannot convert to a CPL now.

The teacher must satisfy the art licensure examination before or during the third year of licensure, and must have attempted it at least once during the first year if it was not passed before the IPL was issued. For art, the required test is Praxis 5135 with a required score of 161.

The Beginning Teacher Support Program requirement can be waived only if the teacher has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina, or previously held a CPL that reverted to an IPL under LICN-030.
An Initial Professional License is a three-year, nonrenewable license.

questions_for_user: Does the teacher's two years count as licensed teaching experience in North Carolina, and when does the teacher expect to reach three years?
Has the teacher already passed the Praxis 5135 art exam (score 161 or higher), and if not, did they attempt it during the first year of the IPL?
Has the teacher completed a Beginning Teacher Support Program, or do they have three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina?
When was the IPL issued? It is nonrenewable and lasts three years, so the timing affects when the teacher must meet the conversion requirements.
premise_corrections: The question assumes the teacher can upgrade now, but the policies require three years of licensed teaching experience, and the teacher has only two.
not_covered: The policies provided do not define 'licensed teaching experience' or say whether partial years count toward it for licensure purposes (LICN-006 addresses experience for salary purposes only).

The policies provided do not say what happens to the teacher's license if the three-year IPL term expires before the conversion requirements are met, beyond the general expiration rule in LICN-003 and LICN-001 §3(g).
The policies provided do not address rules that applied before the current versions took effect on 2026-07-01.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer gives the correct bottom line that two years is short of the three-year CPL requirement, and it covers the exam timing, the Praxis 5135 score of 161, and the BTSP requirement with its exemptions. It omits the peripheral $60 fee point and only implies that holding the IPL satisfies the first condition. All cited claims are backed by the quoted policy text.

question: Teacher with a Birth-K license from NC, working in a private preschool. Does the license cover that setting?

answer.summary: The passages confirm that Birth through Kindergarten is a teacher license area, and that a teacher license entitles the holder to teach in the areas listed on it. They do not address whether that license covers employment in a private preschool. The license-requirement rule applies to public school employment, so the analyst should confirm the private-preschool question against policy outside this set.

claims.text: Birth – Kindergarten is a recognized teacher license area, classified under Elementary.
A teacher license entitles the licensee to teach in the license area(s) indicated on the license.
The general licensure requirement applies to any person employed as a professional educator in a North Carolina public school, and requires a DPI professional educator license.

An Initial Professional License (IPL) and a Continuing Professional License (CPL) each entitle the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina. The passages do not limit this by employer type.
The passages do not say whether a private preschool is a setting the license covers, and they do not define private preschool employment.

question: Teacher is on an RL in special ed, 2 years in, wants to add a general ed K-12 area. Can they do both on one RL?

answer.summary: Adding a general education area to a residency license is not covered by the standard add-on route, which applies only to IPLs and CPLs and expressly excludes residency licenses. The only path the passages provide is a residency license in an additional area, and that requires the applicant to hold a clear license in another area, so the answer depends on what licenses the teacher holds and which general education area is requested.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.
The standard add-on route lets an applicant add a teaching area to an existing IPL or CPL, and an applicant may add to an IPL only if the exam requirements for the initial area are met.
DPI shall not add teaching license areas under the add-on section to a residency license.
A residency license may be requested for an applicant in an additional license area if the applicant holds a clear license in another area and meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) for each requested area.

A clear license is a professional educator license that is in good standing, requires no additional professional examinations or coursework, has no revocation, discipline, or pending unprofessional-conduct investigation, and has not been voluntarily surrendered under investigation.
The passages do not state whether a residency license itself qualifies as a clear license under LICN-001 §2(f) or LICN-019 §4.

Under LICN-019 §1(a), a residency license is issued to an applicant who has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination for that content area.
Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum can be added only by satisfying the applicable licensure examination requirements, not through coursework alone.
Residency license holders may not be issued a permit to teach or emergency license in the same license area.

If the applicant does not qualify for a residency license in the additional area under LICN-019 §4, the passages do not provide any other route in which a residency license could add a general education area.

questions_for_user: Does the teacher hold a clear license in another area, such as a CPL or IPL in a general education area? LICN-019 §4 depends on this, and the passages do not say whether the current residency license counts as clear.

Which specific general education K-12 area is being requested? For example, Elementary (K-6) requires an exam under LICN-013 §2, and secondary or special subject areas have their own exam requirements in LICN-003.
Has the teacher passed the applicable licensure examination for the requested area, or completed 24 credit hours of coursework in it under LICN-019 §1(a)?
Is the teacher's current residency license in Exceptional Children: General Curriculum or another area, and has the teacher already attempted the required exam during the first year of the license?
Is the request from the employing PSU, since LICN-019 §4 requires the governing body of the PSU to make the request?
premise_corrections: The standard add-on process in LICN-013 cannot be used to add an area to a residency license, so the teacher cannot simply add the general education area to the existing RL through that route.
not_covered: The content of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which LICN-019 §4 requires the applicant to meet for each requested area.
Whether a residency license counts as a clear license for purposes of LICN-019 §4, beyond the definition in LICN-001 §2(f).
Whether a general education K-12 area is a recognized license area under LICN-010 or LICN-003, since the passages list specific areas rather than a general K-12 general education area.
Any rule on whether the teacher's special education residency license can be renewed a third time or converted in the context of the new area request beyond LICN-019 §2 and §3.
Any requirements for the 10 days of professional development under LICN-019 §5 in relation to adding an area.

incorrect_statements: Claim 9 implies that no other route exists for a residency license to add a general education area, but the answer key identifies conversion of the RL to an IPL or CPL by June 30 of year three as a route.
The summary says the only path the passages provide is a residency license in an additional area, omitting the RL-to-IPL/CPL conversion route.

question: Teacher's NC CPL expired 3 years ago, now wants to return to teaching at a different district. Options?

answer.summary: The main path is for the new district to request validation of the expired CPL under LICN-033 §3, but only if the teacher was not employed by any PSU in the preceding fiscal year. If validation does not apply, the teacher would need to apply for a new license (IPL under LICN-020, then CPL under LICN-024), and the answer also depends on why the CPL expired.

claims.text: A continuing professional license is a five-year renewable license, and every license expires on June 30 of its expiration year unless it is renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy.

A PSU governing body may ask DPI to validate an expired CPL for an applicant under its employment, even without the required CEUs, but only if the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year.
A validated CPL is effective for three years. To renew it for a new five-year cycle, the educator must complete the renewal requirements in LICN-030 (teachers) by the end of the third year.

Teachers renewing a CPL through the employing LEA must have evidence of at least 'proficient' on their most recent annual evaluation, with proficient on Standard 4 and on three of five standards. Teachers must also complete 8 CEUs per cycle: 4 in license area and 4 general for grades 6-12, or 3 in license area, 3 literacy, and 2 general for PreK-5.
Validating an expired CPL, opened by the employing school system, carries a $60 fee. An in-state initial professional license application opened by the individual carries a $70 fee.

If a teacher's CPL expired because the teacher met the renewal criteria but was not placed on a mandatory improvement plan, the license expires at the end of the renewal cycle, and the teacher may apply for an IPL 30 days after receiving DPI's notice of expiration.

An applicant may qualify for an IPL if they completed a recognized NC educator preparation program and are recommended by the EPP, or completed an EPP outside NC, or hold a clear out-of-state license and have fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction. A PSU may request an IPL for an applicant who completed all NC EPP requirements but has not passed the licensure exam, without EPP recommendation.

To qualify for a CPL, a teacher must hold an NC IPL or residency license, satisfy exam requirements (attempted during the first year of the IPL if not passed before it was issued, and passed before or during the third year), have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless exempt, including exemption for a previously held CPL that reverted to an IPL under LICN-030.
Applications for licensure services, other than renewal, must be submitted by April 15 to guarantee processing before the end of the fiscal year (July 1 through June 30).

Reinstatement under LICN-007 §8 applies only to licenses revoked or applications denied under that policy, with petitions allowed no sooner than 12 months after the revocation or denial. It does not address licenses that expired.

questions_for_user: Why did the CPL expire? Was it non-renewal for missing CEUs, a failed evaluation, a mandatory improvement plan outcome, or something else?
Was the teacher employed by any NC public school unit during the fiscal year immediately before the new district's request? This decides whether LICN-033 §3 validation is available.
Has the teacher held any other NC professional educator license since the CPL expired?
Did the teacher complete a recognized NC educator preparation program, and at what degree level?
How many years of licensed teaching experience does the teacher have, in NC and in any other state?
Has the teacher passed the required licensure exam for the license area, and when?
Does the teacher have any discipline, investigation, or pending criminal matter reported to DPI?
Is the new district planning to request the license before April 15?
not_covered: Whether a CPL expired three years ago can still be validated. The passages give no time limit for validation under LICN-033 §3.
Whether the teacher's expired CPL can be reinstated directly, without validation or a new application.
Any effect of the three-year gap on the teacher's prior experience credit for salary purposes beyond the general rules in LICN-006.
Rules for transfers between districts for a license that has expired.
The policies provided are current versions only (effective 2026-07-01 or later for most). They cannot confirm what rules applied when the CPL expired three years ago.

incorrect_statements: If validation does not apply, the teacher would need to apply for a new license (IPL under LICN-020, then CPL under LICN-024). The cited policies do not establish this as a route for an expired NC CPL holder, and the answer key says no general reinstatement path exists.
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly identifies LICN-033 §3 validation, its three-year effect, the employment-history threshold, and the renewal requirements, and its citations support nearly all claims. It loses credit for asserting an IPL-then-CPL fallback that the policies do not clearly provide for this situation, and it omits the fee-table currency caveat.

question: Applicant has a 2-year community college associate degree in early childhood and wants to teach pre-K in a public school. Which license?

answer.summary: Based on the passages, an associate degree alone does not qualify this applicant for a standard teacher license in Birth-Kindergarten (pre-K) at a North Carolina public school. The applicant would need at least a bachelor's-level educator preparation program for a teacher license, and the permit and emergency license paths also require a bachelor's degree. Whether a residency license is possible turns on a statute the passages do not include, so confirm the bachelor's status and that statute before advising.

claims.text: A teacher license generally requires completion of an educator preparation program at the Bachelor's (A-Level), Master's, Specialist, or Doctoral level.

An applicant with only a high school diploma or an associate's degree (V-Level) may be issued a teacher license only in Career and Technical Education, Junior Reserve Officer Training Corps, or Safety and Driver Education. Birth-Kindergarten is not one of these areas.
Birth through Kindergarten is a recognized teacher license classification (pre-K falls within it), but the passages do not state that it can be issued on an associate's degree.

The Pre-School Add-On cannot be issued as a standalone license. It can only be added to an existing license in Elementary Education, Special Education, or Family and Consumer Sciences – General, under LICN-013.

A Permit to Teach requires the applicant to hold at least a bachelor's degree and never have held another North Carolina professional educator license. This applicant does not meet the degree requirement based on the facts given.

An Emergency License requires at least a bachelor's degree with at least 18 credit hours relevant to the licensure area, and no completed recognized educator preparation program in that area. This applicant does not meet the degree requirement based on the facts given.

A Residency License requires the applicant to meet G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and to have either 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination. The statute is not in the passages, so the applicant's eligibility under it cannot be determined here.
The degree level on a license is based on the highest degree from an educator preparation program, and an applicant is only eligible for a license at the highest level at which they completed an EPP.

questions_for_user: Does the applicant hold any bachelor's degree (from any institution), and if so, did they complete a recognized educator preparation program at the bachelor's level, including in early childhood?
Has the applicant ever held any North Carolina professional educator license, such as a permit, emergency, or residency license?
Has the applicant been hired by a North Carolina public school unit? If so, has the unit requested a residency or emergency license on their behalf?
Does the applicant meet G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5)? That statute is not in the passages, so the answer needs to come from the statute itself.
premise_corrections: The question assumes a 2-year associate degree is enough for a pre-K teaching license. The passages allow associate's-degree holders to be licensed to teach only in CTE, JROTC, and Safety and Driver Education (LICN-010 §4), and Birth-Kindergarten is not on that list.
not_covered: The content of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which governs residency license eligibility and therefore whether a residency license is possible.
Whether pre-K positions in public schools have any requirement beyond the license classification.
Whether the associate degree could count toward experience or salary credit (LICN-006 addresses experience credit, not licensure eligibility).
Any requirements in effect before the 2026-07-01 effective dates of the current policies.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line that an associate degree does not qualify for a pre-K teacher license, and its cited policy text backs nearly all claims. It omits that the LICN-010 §2 degree rule may extend to residency and that Birth-Kindergarten has no required exam, and claim 2 rests on a bare list heading.

question: Applicant from Tennessee, 7 yrs teaching special ed, has a current TN license but it's in a different category than NC EC. Which NC license fits?

answer.summary: With 7 years of experience, the applicant falls under the out-of-state CPL route in LICN-025 §2, not the IPL route. The passages do not map Tennessee's special education category to a North Carolina Exceptional Children area, so the specific NC license cannot be determined without the Tennessee license category and the criteria below.

claims.text: An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a continuing professional license under LICN-025 §2. An applicant with 7 years of experience is above that threshold, so the IPL route in LICN-025 §1(a), which covers applicants with fewer than three years, does not apply.
To qualify for the CPL under LICN-025 §2, the applicant must meet both LICN-025 §2(a) and LICN-025 §2(b).

LICN-025 §2(a) requires that the applicant hold a clear license from another jurisdiction. For this policy, a clear license must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, free of any pending unprofessional-conduct investigation relating to the license, and not voluntarily surrendered while under investigation.

LICN-025 §2(b) is satisfied if the applicant holds National Board for Professional Teaching Standards certification, or if Tennessee's licensure requirements are substantially similar to North Carolina's. Substantially similar means Tennessee required, at minimum, completion of an educator preparation program recognized by the state where it is located, and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought.
The passages provided do not say whether Tennessee's requirements meet the substantially similar test or whether the applicant has National Board certification.

The applicant's license must be for a North Carolina license area under LICN-010. Exceptional Children areas include General Curriculum, Adapted Curriculum, Learning Disabled, Cross Categorical, Severely/Profoundly Disabled, Mentally Disabled, Academically or Intellectually Gifted, Deaf and Hard of Hearing, Visually Impaired, and Behaviorally/Emotionally Disabled.

The passages do not map Tennessee license categories to North Carolina Exceptional Children areas. The correct NC area therefore depends on the Tennessee category and its endorsement scope, which the analyst must supply.

For the CPL based on an out-of-state clear license, the applicant must present evidence of out-of-state exam results at the time of initial NC licensure. An out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

The NC exam requirements for Exceptional Children areas are listed in LICN-003. For example, Special Education: General Curriculum (88091) requires Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with a score of 145, or Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with a score of 233, plus a math subtest. Adapted Curriculum (88092) requires Severe to Profound Tests 5547 and 5511. These apply to NC licensure only if the policy requires them for the applicant's license, and the LICN-025 §2(b)(ii) out-of-state exam route is the relevant alternative.
The passages do not say whether the applicant has taken or passed the required NC or Tennessee exams for the target area.

Is the Tennessee license currently in good standing, renewable by Tennessee, and free of any discipline, revocation, or pending unprofessional-conduct investigation?

Does the applicant have a passing score on the relevant NC exam or Tennessee exam for the target EC area?
not_covered: Mapping of Tennessee license categories to North Carolina Exceptional Children license areas.
Whether Tennessee's licensure requirements are substantially similar to North Carolina's.
Tennessee's exam requirements and cut scores.

Any Tennessee-specific licensure recognition rules outside the LICN policy series, including the Veterans Auto and Education Improvement Act provisions, which apply only to servicemembers and spouses.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line: the out-of-state CPL route under LICN-025 §2, the clear-license and substantially-similar/NBPTS criteria, and no Tennessee-to-NC Exceptional Children crosswalk, so needs_more_info. It omits the rule on adding further areas after issuance (LICN-025 §4 and LICN-013), which is peripheral, and claim 5's 'must be for an NC area' overstates what the cited §5(b) says.

answer.summary: The passages do not mention Praxis Core, so they cannot confirm that the 2015 Praxis Core scores count toward a residency license. question: School nurse with an RN and MSN, no teaching license. Does NC have a school nurse license or cert?

answer.summary: The LICN policies provided do not establish a school nurse license or certificate. The only student services personnel license classifications are school counselor, school social worker, school psychologist, media coordinator, and instructional technology specialist-telecommunications, and school nurse is not among them.

claims.text: The student services personnel license classifications are School Counselor, School Social Worker, School Psychologist, Media Coordinator, and Instructional Technology Specialist-Telecommunications. School nurse is not listed.

Student services personnel are defined as individuals providing specialized assistance to students, teachers, administrators, or the education program, and the definition lists school counseling, school social work, school psychology, audiology, speech-language pathology, and media coordination. School nursing is not named.

A professional educator is an administrator, teacher, or student services personnel. Any person employed as a professional educator in a NC public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, a DPI professional educator license under SBE policy.

The SBE testing requirements table lists no school nurse license area. The student services entries are school counselor, school psychologist, media coordinator, audiologist, and speech-language pathologist.

If a role were a covered student services classification, the license requires completion of an educator preparation program at the master's level or higher, and the applicant is eligible only at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP. The policies provided do not say whether an RN or MSN in nursing counts as completing an EPP.

question: Applicant with BS in psych from NC school, currently in a counseling masters program, 1 yr done. Eligible for an RL as school counselor yet?

answer.summary: Based on the current policies, this applicant does not qualify for a residency license as a school counselor yet. The residency license is defined by LICN-019, which is written for teachers, and the student services license requires a completed master's-level educator preparation program that the applicant has not yet finished.

claims.text: A residency license is defined as a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.
School counselor is a student services personnel classification, and student services personnel are separate from teachers.

The student services personnel license classifications in LICN-012 are School Counselor, School Social Worker, School Psychologist, Media Coordinator, and Instructional Technology Specialist-Telecommunications. LICN-012 does not list a residency license as a student services option.
LICN-019 governs residency licenses and refers to a teacher holding a residency license. Residency is listed among the teacher license classifications in LICN-010.

To qualify for a student services personnel license, an applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the master's, specialist, or doctoral level. Completion is required, and the applicant is one year into a program that is not yet complete.

Even on the teacher residency track, eligibility requires a PSU governing body request and either 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passing the applicable licensure examination for that content area.

A student services personnel applicant must pass any applicable licensure exam before or during the third year of licensure, and must attempt it at least once during the first year. If the exam is not passed before applying, the applicant receives an initial professional license rather than a continuing one.

It does not state that enrollment alone is not disqualifying, which is a peripheral point.

question: Teacher is on an RL in math 6-9 and wants to add a math 9-12 area. Has 15 semester hours in math beyond their degree. Does that work?

answer.summary: Assuming RL means residency license, the policies do not let DPI add a new teaching area to a residency license through coursework, so the 15 semester hours do not get the teacher the 9-12 math area by that route. Even apart from that bar, 15 hours is short of the 24 required for the coursework path, so the teacher would need to pursue a different route, such as a residency license in the added area under LICN-019 §4, which depends on facts not provided.

claims.text: LICN-013 allows an applicant to add a new license area to an existing initial professional license or continuing professional license, not to a residency license.
LICN-013 §3(c) states that DPI shall not add additional teaching license areas under Section 1 to a Residency License, so the coursework route is closed for a residency license holder.

Even for an eligible license type, the coursework route requires 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area, with a grade of C or better in each course. Fifteen semester hours is 9 hours short of 24 (24 − 15 = 9).
LICN-013 refers to credit hours, not semester hours. The policies provided do not state whether semester hours are counted the same way, but the 15 hours is below 24 under either reading.

A residency license may be requested for an additional license area if the applicant holds a clear license in another area and meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) for each requested area. This is a separate route from LICN-013.
A clear license is a license that does not require completion of any additional professional examinations or coursework, is in good standing, and has no discipline or pending investigation.
A residency license in a content area requires either at least 24 hours of coursework in that content area or passing the applicable licensure examination for that content area.
The Praxis 9-12 Mathematics test is code 5165 with a required score of 159.
Adding a license area by passing the required exam is governed by LICN-013 §1(a), which is also barred on a residency license by LICN-013 §3(c).

question: lapsed NC CPL 8 months, wants to sub while reinstating. what can they do

answer.summary: The policies provided do not provide a reinstatement route for a lapsed CPL. The only applicable path is a request by the employing PSU for DPI to validate the expired CPL, and it is available only if the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year. Whether substitute work is covered by a license requirement is not addressed.

claims.text: The policies provided contain no reinstatement process for a lapsed CPL. LICN-007 §8 covers reinstatement only for a license that was revoked or an application that was denied under LICN-007, and it is not triggered by an ordinary lapse.

A PSU governing body may request that DPI validate an expired CPL issued to an applicant under its employment, even if the educator lacks the required CEUs, but only if the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year.

A validated CPL is effective for three years. To renew it for a new five-year cycle, the educator must complete the relevant renewal requirements from LICN-030, LICN-031, or LICN-032 by the end of the third year.
Opening a validation of an expired CPL, when opened by the employing school system on behalf of the educator, carries a fee of $60.

Every license expires on June 30 of the calendar year in which it is set to expire unless it is renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy. A CPL that is 8 months past its expiration therefore falls under the expired-license validation rule.

A CEU is either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from a higher education institution or ten clock hours of professional development. This is the basis for converting any coursework into CEUs.
Service as a substitute teacher is not recognized for professional educator experience credit for salary purposes.
Any person employed as a professional educator in a NC public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, a professional educator license.

question: Teacher holds a CPL in elementary ed and now wants to be a district media coordinator. Has a master's in library science. Does the CPL plus MLS qualify?

answer.summary: A media coordinator is a student services personnel role, which requires a student services personnel license, not a teacher license. The CPL in elementary education alone does not establish eligibility, and the MLS qualifies only if it was completed through a recognized educator preparation program at the master's level and the Praxis 5312 requirement is met.

claims.text: Media coordinator is classified as student services personnel, and a student services personnel license is a separate license classification from the teacher license.
A teacher CPL is a license in the teacher classification, and the passages list the teacher and student services personnel classifications separately.
To qualify for a student services personnel license, an applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the master's, specialist, or doctoral level.

An applicant is only eligible for a license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP. If the MLS was completed through an EPP at the master's level, the master's level is the applicable level.

A degree from a program that is not an educator preparation program does not satisfy the EPP requirement. The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where it is based.
The required licensure test for Media Coordinator (code 076) is Praxis 5312 with a required score of 154.

A student services personnel applicant must satisfy any applicable licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, and must attempt the examination at least once during the first year if it was not passed before the initial application.

A continuing professional license for administrator or student services personnel requires satisfying the applicable examination requirements and meeting the other requirements of LICN-011 or LICN-012.
The Media Supervisor role is listed under Administrative/Supervisory with its own code (078) and test (Praxis 5412, score 146), so the exact job title matters for which license path applies.
The policy passages provided do not describe a way for a teacher CPL to be converted or added to a student services personnel license. The add-on rule (LICN-013) covers teaching license areas only.

questions_for_user: Was the MLS completed through an educator preparation program recognized by the SBE (or the equivalent licensing authority in the state where the program is based), or through a general graduate program?
Has the teacher already passed the Praxis 5312 Media Coordinator test with a score of at least 154, or does the teacher still need to take it?
Is the position a media coordinator (student services personnel) or a media supervisor (administrator)? The license path differs.
Does the teacher hold any student services personnel license now, or only the teacher CPL?
Does the teacher's MLS-based application fall within the first year of licensure for test timing purposes, or has the teacher already held a student services personnel license?
premise_corrections: The question assumes that a CPL in elementary education plus an MLS qualifies the teacher for a district media coordinator role. The passages classify media coordinator as student services personnel, which requires a student services personnel license. A teacher CPL is a teacher-classification license, and the passages do not say it carries over to student services personnel.
not_covered: Whether a master's in library science is treated as an educator preparation program in North Carolina or in the state where it was earned.
Any conversion or add-on path from a teacher CPL directly to a student services personnel license.
Whether graduate pay under LICN-006 applies to an MLS in this situation, beyond the general criteria.
Any specific NC standards for library science or media coordinator coursework.
Any prior rules that applied before the current version's effective date.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the key's bottom line that the CPL alone does not qualify and that eligibility turns on an SBE-recognized master's-level EPP plus Praxis 5312 at 154. Its citations support nearly all claims, though claim 1 does not show a CPL is a teacher-classification license and claim 9 overstates what LICN-013 says. It omits the LICN-006 §V salary-versus-eligibility nuance and the no-extra-coursework point, which are peripheral.

question: Candidate completed NBPTS in middle grades math, currently holds an RL. Can NBC move them to CPL early?

answer.summary: National Board certification is not a listed basis for converting a Residency License to a CPL in the provided policies, so it does not by itself allow an early move to CPL. The candidate can convert only by meeting the ordinary CPL requirements (licensed teaching experience, exam requirements, Beginning Teacher Support Program unless exempt, and EPP recommendation) within the residency timeline.

claims.text: A Residency License converts to an IPL or CPL only if the applicant meets the requirements of LICN-020 (IPL) or LICN-024 (CPL) and is recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

To qualify for a CPL, a teacher must hold an NC initial professional or residency license, satisfy the licensure examination requirements, have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies. National Board certification is not listed as an exception.

The BTSP exception applies only to applicants with at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina, or to those who previously held a CPL that reverted to an IPL. Neither applies to a candidate who currently holds an NC Residency License based on the facts given.

A residency conversion is timed as follows: if the requirements are met by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not met by that date, the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL is effective on the date the requirements are met.
A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice.

National Board certification is addressed in the policies only as (a) an application document, where proof is required if applicable, and (b) a CEU credit for the renewal cycle in which certification is received, which is an 8-CEU credit for a CPL renewal. Neither provision provides a route to convert a Residency License to a CPL.

CEU arithmetic for reference: a teacher renewing a CPL in Grades 6 through 12 must complete 8 CEUs per five-year cycle, and one CEU equals ten clock hours of professional development or two-thirds of a semester credit hour. National Board certification credits all 8 CEUs for the cycle in which it is received, so the candidate's CEU requirement for that cycle would be fully satisfied. This affects CPL renewal, not conversion.
The out-of-state National Board pathway in LICN-025 applies to applicants holding a clear license from another jurisdiction, not to a holder of an NC Residency License.

questions_for_user: How many years of licensed teaching experience does the candidate have? A CPL requires at least three.
How long has the candidate held the Residency License, and which year of the residency is it now? This determines the June 30 third-year deadline.
Has the candidate passed the applicable licensure exam for Middle Grades Mathematics (Praxis 5164 per the LICN-003 table), or is that still pending?
Did the candidate complete the Beginning Teacher Support Program, or do they qualify for an exception?
Will the candidate's EPP recommend them for the CPL?
Was any prior teaching done outside North Carolina that might count toward the out-of-state experience exception?
premise_corrections: The question assumes National Board certification can move a Residency License holder to a CPL early. The provided policies do not list National Board certification as a conversion basis. National Board certification affects CEU credit for CPL renewal (LICN-033 §2) and is an application document (LICN-004 §1(j)), not an early conversion route.
not_covered: Whether DPI has any unpublished or separate procedure allowing early conversion based on National Board certification.
Any pre-July 2026 rules on residency-to-CPL conversion or National Board treatment; the policies provided cannot confirm what applied before their current effective dates.
The specific NC Middle Grades Mathematics exam score requirement for the candidate, beyond the LICN-003 table reference.
Whether the candidate's employing PSU has requested or can request any conversion on the candidate's behalf beyond the requirements listed here.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer gives the correct bottom line that National Board certification is not a conversion route and that the CPL requirements (three years' experience, exams, BTSP, EPP recommendation) and June 30 timing still govern. Its claims are backed by the cited policy text, though it omits the explicit three-year condition on the out-of-state NBC alternative.

question: Teacher on RL in agriculture CTE, 2 yrs in, wants to earn a CPL. Has 3 years of industry experience besides teaching. Does that count?

answer.summary: The 3 years of industry experience do not count toward the CPL's three-year licensed teaching requirement. The teacher has 2 years of licensed teaching, so the CPL is not available yet; they need a third year of licensed teaching plus the other CPL requirements. Industry experience may earn salary experience credit under LICN-006 Section II if the PSU recommends it and it meets the criteria, but that is separate from CPL eligibility.

claims.text: To qualify for a continuing professional teacher license, an applicant must hold an IPL or residency license in North Carolina, satisfy the licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure (attempting them at least once in the first year if not already satisfied before the IPL), have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

The CPL requirement is three years of licensed teaching experience. The policy does not count non-teaching or industry work toward that requirement; LICN-024 requires licensed teaching experience specifically.

Non-teaching work experience is credited for salary purposes only, toward the individual's total licensure experience rating, on the recommendation of the employing PSU's personnel administrator. It is not described as satisfying CPL qualification requirements.

Non-teaching experience qualifies for salary credit only if it was at least half-time (20 or more hours per week), was completed after age 18, did not include on-the-job training, was paid and documented, and is directly related to the area of licensure or work assignment as found by DPI's Licensure Section.

Salary credit for non-teaching experience is one year of credit for every two years of full-time relevant experience completed before the bachelor's degree, and one year for every year of full-time relevant experience completed after the bachelor's degree. For the teacher's 3 industry years, if all were full-time, relevant, and completed after the bachelor's degree, the arithmetic is 3 years x 1 credit = 3 salary experience years. If completed before the bachelor's degree, the arithmetic is 3 years / 2 = 1.5 credit years, which would be combined with partial years under the policy's combination rule.

Experience credit for an agriculture CTE teacher may differ: the one-year-per-year rule for Class V Career-Technical Trade and Industry licenses applies only after the individual completed required training and work experience for the provisional license. The policies provided do not state whether agriculture CTE is a Class V license area.

A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued under LICN-019. To convert a residency license to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL or CPL requirements and be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee. Conversion requirements must be met by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, or the residency license expires.

Renewing a residency license requires that the applicant be enrolled in a recognized EPP, be employed as a teacher in the PSU, have at least six months of teaching experience in the preceding school year, and complete 10 days of professional development in the first year of the residency license.

The CPL requirement for licensed teaching experience applies to the teacher's time on licensed teaching status, and the policies provided do not define whether time on a residency license counts as licensed teaching experience for the CPL requirement.

questions_for_user: Has the teacher already satisfied the licensure examination requirements for agriculture CTE, or will they test in the second or third year?
Is the teacher enrolled in and recommended by a recognized EPP, as required for residency renewal and conversion?
Has the teacher completed or been exempted from the Beginning Teacher Support Program?
Did the 3 years of industry experience occur before or after the bachelor's degree, and were they full-time (20 or more hours per week), paid, documented, and not on-the-job training?
Has the PSU recommended the industry experience for salary credit, and does it relate directly to agriculture CTE?
Does the teacher have any prior licensed teaching experience in another state or in NC, and when did the residency license start?
premise_corrections: The question assumes the 3 years of industry experience might count toward the CPL. The policies say the CPL requires three years of licensed teaching experience, which industry work does not supply.
not_covered: Whether time on a residency license counts as licensed teaching experience for the CPL three-year requirement, since the policies do not define licensed teaching experience.
Whether agriculture CTE is a Class V Career-Technical Trade and Industry license area.
The exact salary experience credit the teacher would receive, since that depends on facts not provided.
Any rules for CTE-specific provisional licenses or Career-Technical Education Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual requirements, which the policies reference but do not include.
Earlier rules in effect before the current versions.

incorrect_statements: The summary states as fact that the teacher has 2 years of licensed teaching, which assumes residency-license service counts toward the CPL experience requirement. The policies do not establish this, and the answer itself later says it is undefined.
metrics.judge_rationale: The bottom line that industry experience does not count toward the CPL's three years of licensed teaching is correct and well cited. The answer does, however, assume that residency-license years count as licensed teaching, which it elsewhere admits the policies do not define, and it hedges somewhat on the agriculture CTE Class V question.

question: Teacher has 4 years on an Emergency License in middle grades science, still no ed degree. Can they stay on it another year?

answer.summary: No. An Emergency License is one-year and nonrenewable, valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year requested, and it cannot be extended, so the teacher cannot stay on it another year. If the teacher still needs a license, the passages point to a residency license requested by the employing school unit, which depends on coursework or test results the analyst has not yet confirmed.

claims.text: An Emergency License (EL) is defined as a one-year nonrenewable license issued to an individual who meets the requirements of LICN-018.
An Emergency License is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested, and it cannot be extended or renewed.

Every license expires on June 30 of the calendar year in which it is set to expire, unless it is renewed, extended, or converted to another type of license under SBE policy. Because the EL cannot be renewed or extended, the policies do not provide a path to keep it past its expiration.

A person may receive an Emergency License only if they hold a bachelor's degree with at least 18 credit hours of relevant coursework, have not completed a recognized educator preparation program in that licensure area, and do not qualify for a residency license.
A person who holds or previously held a residency license cannot receive an Emergency License in the same license area.

A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019. The governing body of a public school unit may request one for an applicant under its employment if the applicant meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination for that content area.
For middle grades science, the policies list the Praxis 5442 test with a required score of 152.

Because the residency license is not available if the applicant does not qualify for it under LICN-019, the teacher's coursework and test status determine whether a residency license is an option. Renewing a residency license requires enrollment in a recognized educator preparation program, employment as a teacher in the PSU, at least six months of teaching experience in the preceding school year, and 10 days of professional development in the first year.

questions_for_user: Has the teacher completed at least 24 semester hours of coursework in middle grades science, or passed the Praxis 5442 with a score of 152 or higher?
Is the teacher currently enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program?
Does the employing school unit intend to request a residency license for this teacher?
When does the current Emergency License expire, and what fiscal year was it requested for?
premise_corrections: The premise that the teacher has held an Emergency License for 4 years conflicts with the policies. An Emergency License is a one-year nonrenewable license valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year requested, and it cannot be extended or renewed. Any earlier Emergency License issuance or renewal would not match the current rules, and the policies provided cannot confirm what applied before their current effective date of 2026-07-01.
not_covered: What rules applied to Emergency Licenses before the current effective date (2026-07-01), including whether multi-year Emergency Licenses were ever allowed.
The statutory text of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which sets the residency license eligibility requirement and is not reproduced in the passages.
Whether a teacher on an expired Emergency License can be issued a different license type, beyond the general expiration rule in LICN-001 §3(g).
Whether the Praxis 5442 score requirement or the 24-hour coursework option is currently accepted for this specific teacher's coursework, since the transcripts were not provided.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer gives the key's bottom line that the teacher cannot stay on the Emergency License another year, and it covers the residency alternative, the 24-hour and Praxis 5442 (152) options, and the EPP renewal condition. Each claim is backed by the policy text it cites, and it flags the four-year history as conflicting with the one-year definition.

question: Applicant has a master's in TESOL from a university in the UK and 4 years teaching ESL in London. Which NC license applies?

answer.summary: Because the applicant has more than three years of licensed experience, the out-of-state IPL route does not fit. The likely path is an out-of-state Continuing Professional License for teacher, ESL, under LICN-025 Section 2, if the applicant holds a clear UK license and either holds NBPTS certification or the UK requirements are substantially similar to NC's (EPP plus a passing exam score in ESL). Confirm the UK license status, whether the TESOL master's came from a recognized EPP, and any UK exam results before choosing a license.

claims.text: The applicant is an out-of-state applicant because the master's was completed with a principal place of business outside North Carolina, and this definition expressly includes international preparation programs.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an IPL. The applicant's 4 years of ESL teaching in London is more than three years, so this IPL route does not fit if the experience was licensed.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a CPL. The applicant must meet both criteria: (a) hold a clear license from another jurisdiction, and (b) either hold NBPTS certification or have licensure requirements in that jurisdiction substantially similar to NC's.

A clear license for this purpose must be in good standing, be renewable by the issuing authority, not be revoked or disciplined, have no pending unprofessional-conduct investigation in any state, and not have been voluntarily surrendered while under investigation.

Substantially similar means the other jurisdiction required, at minimum, completion of an EPP recognized by the state where the EPP is located, and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought. Without both, the NBPTS route is the only CPL route.

The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business. A UK master's in TESOL counts toward licensure only if the program meets this test. A TESOL master's does not qualify simply by its subject; the program must be an EPP.
Exam evidence must be presented at initial licensure in NC. An out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

A teacher license at the master's level requires completion of an EPP at the M-Level. The license degree level is the highest degree from which the applicant completed an EPP, and the teacher license classification must match this level.
English as a Second Language is a K-12 special subject teaching license area in NC.

For the NC ESL license area (code 110), the NC-required test is Praxis 5362 with a required score of 155. Whether a UK exam can substitute for this test is not addressed in the passages, except that out-of-state exams must be a passing score in the examining jurisdiction for the license area.
A CPL shall entitle the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in NC.

Teacher CPL initial criteria under NC rules also require a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless the applicant has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside NC. The applicant's 4 years of experience in London would satisfy that exception if licensed.

questions_for_user: Does the applicant hold a current, renewable UK teaching license that is in good standing, with no discipline, pending investigation, or voluntary surrender?
Were the 4 years in London served under that UK license (licensed experience), and is the count exact?
Did the TESOL master's come from a program recognized as an EPP by the UK authority that leads to teacher licensure?
Does the applicant hold NBPTS certification?
If not NBPTS, did the UK license require completion of an EPP and a passing score on a UK exam in ESL, and what was the score?
Is the applicant seeking the license as a K-12 ESL teacher (license area 110/ESL)?
Does the applicant hold any NC license now or previously?
not_covered: Whether the UK licensing authority recognizes the TESOL master's program as an EPP, or how UK licensing works in general.
Whether a UK exam score can be treated as equivalent to NC Praxis 5362 at score 155 for ESL, beyond the 'passing score' language of LICN-025.
The NC application fee for an out-of-state CPL; LICN-008 lists only an out-of-state IPL fee ($100).
Whether the 4 years of London teaching count as licensed experience for NC purposes if the applicant was unlicensed there.
Salary placement or graduate pay for the master's under LICN-006, since the question concerns licensure only.
Any policy before the current effective dates (2026-07-01 for most of these rules).

incorrect_statements: The IPL route is said not to fit at all because of 4 years of experience, but LICN-020 §1(b) has no experience limit and was not considered.
Claim 4 says that without both criteria the NBPTS route is the only CPL route, which misreads the either/or structure of LICN-025 §2(b).
metrics.judge_rationale: The answer correctly identifies the out-of-state status, the M-level and EPP requirements, the CPL route, the clear-license criteria, and the ESL test score, and it asks for the right facts. It omits the application and fee, alternative permit/residency/emergency licenses, and the graduate pay point, and it dismisses the IPL route without considering LICN-020 §1(b).

question: Teacher wants a Permit to Teach in CTE cosmetology. Has a state cosmetology license and 6 years of work experience. Qualify?

answer.summary: Whether the teacher qualifies for a Permit to Teach turns mainly on whether they hold at least a bachelor's degree; the 6 years of work experience is not a criterion for the permit. The cosmetology license does not appear to bar the permit, since the bar is for prior NC professional educator licenses, but the passages do not confirm that the cosmetology license is not one.

claims.text: A PSU governing body may request a Permit to Teach for an applicant under its employment only if the applicant holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license.
The bachelor's degree is a mandatory condition for a Permit to Teach. An applicant without a bachelor's degree does not meet LICN-017 §1(a), so the permit cannot be requested for them.

The 'never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license' condition in LICN-017 §1(b) applies to licenses defined as professional educator licenses issued by DPI. A license is defined as a professional educator license issued by DPI under SBE policy and Chapter 115C, Article 17E.

The policies provided do not say what a state cosmetology license is or who issues it. If it was issued by DPI as a professional educator license, the teacher would fail LICN-017 §1(b). The analyst should confirm the issuing authority.

Six years of work experience is not a condition of the Permit to Teach. The permit is issued at the same pay level as a bachelor's-degree (A-Level) teacher with zero years of experience, regardless of prior work experience.
A Permit to Teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

CTE is a teaching license area that can be issued to applicants with a high school diploma or associate's degree, provided they meet all other requirements for the license classification sought. This does not override the bachelor's degree requirement stated in LICN-017 for the permit classification.

The policies provided do not list cosmetology as a CTE license area. The CTE list in LICN-010 §6(f) does not include cosmetology, and the CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual referenced in LICN-003 is not among the passages.

questions_for_user: Does the teacher hold at least a bachelor's degree, and from what institution? This is the deciding factor.
Who issued the state cosmetology license? If it is a DPI professional educator license, the permit is barred under LICN-017 §1(b).
Has the teacher ever held any other North Carolina professional educator license, such as an IPL, CPL, residency, or limited license?
Is cosmetology an approved CTE license area for the school system? The provided policies do not list it.
premise_corrections: The question implies 6 years of work experience may help qualify the teacher for a Permit to Teach. Under LICN-017, experience is not a condition of the permit, and permit pay is set at the zero-experience A-Level regardless of prior experience.
not_covered: Whether cosmetology is a recognized CTE license area or what its specific requirements are (the CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual is not provided).
What a state cosmetology license is, which agency issues it, and whether it counts as a professional educator license.
Any CTE-specific testing or coursework requirements for cosmetology.

Whether the teacher's 6 years of work experience could support a different license (for example, through LICN-006 non-teaching work experience credit or an emergency license) and what that would require.

incorrect_statements: Claim 6 says the LICN-010 CTE high school diploma or associate's degree option does not override the LICN-017 bachelor's requirement for a permit, which resolves a conflict the policies do not resolve.
metrics.judge_rationale: The bottom line of needs_more_info and the core eligibility points (bachelor's degree, no prior NC professional educator license, DPI definition, zero-experience A-Level pay, June 30 validity) are correct and well supported. However, the answer asserts a resolution of the LICN-010 versus LICN-017 degree conflict that the policies do not provide, and it only implies rather than states that no CTE-specific credential is required.

question: Teacher is a CPL holder in K-12 music who moved from Alabama 6 months ago with an Alabama Class A. Which NC license now?

answer.summary: The NC license depends on how many years of licensed experience the teacher has and whether the Alabama Class A is a clear license under NC's definition. With under three years, the teacher likely gets an NC Initial Professional License (IPL); with more than three years and a qualifying clear license, a Continuing Professional License (CPL) may be possible. The passages do not say whether an Alabama Class A meets the clear-license definition.

claims.text: The passages do not describe an Alabama 'Class A' license or state whether it is equivalent to a clear license under NC rules, so its status must be confirmed against the LICN-025 definition.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an Initial Professional License if they hold a license in the corresponding license area in another jurisdiction, or completed an EPP recognized where it is located.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a CPL only if they hold a clear license from another jurisdiction and either hold National Board certification or the other jurisdiction's requirements are substantially similar to NC's (completion of a recognized EPP and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought).

A 'clear license' under LICN-025 §2(a) must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, with no pending unprofessional-conduct investigation, and not surrendered under investigation.

For an IPL in a license area other than Elementary or Special Education: General Curriculum, the teacher must either pass an out-of-state exam for that area in the examining jurisdiction, or satisfy the applicable NC exam before or during the third year of licensure, having attempted it at least once in the first year.

For K-12 Music, the NC licensure exam is Praxis 5114 with a required score of 162. The out-of-state exam results must be presented at the time of initial NC licensure, and an out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.

Under LICN-024, a CPL based on a clear license from another jurisdiction must meet the LICN-025 requirements, and the NC CPL route based on NC teaching experience requires an IPL or residency license first plus three years of licensed teaching experience.

The passages do not say whether the teacher currently holds an NC license. Because the teacher moved from Alabama, the 'CPL holder' description may refer to the Alabama license, and the NC license type can't be confirmed from what was provided.

questions_for_user: How many years of licensed professional educator experience does the teacher have, counting the Alabama experience? Under three years points to an IPL; more than three points to a possible CPL.

Is the Alabama Class A a current, renewable license that is in good standing, with no discipline or pending investigation? Does Alabama require a substantially similar set of requirements, including an EPP and an exam pass in music?
Did the teacher complete an EPP, and where? Was the EPP recognized by Alabama or its jurisdiction?
Has the teacher passed an Alabama music exam with a score, or any other out-of-state exam? If not, has the teacher taken Praxis 5114 (required score 162)?
Does the teacher hold National Board certification?
Is the teacher a servicemember or the spouse of one? If so, LICN-028 may provide a separate recognition path that was not reviewed here.
Is the teacher's NC employment with a PSU already in place, and what license is the PSU requesting?
premise_corrections: The question calls the teacher a 'CPL holder,' but the teacher moved from Alabama holding an Alabama Class A. Nothing in the passages shows an NC CPL has been issued, so the NC license has to be determined from the LICN-025 out-of-state rules.
not_covered: Whether an Alabama Class A license is equivalent to an NC clear license or to an Alabama license that NC recognizes.
Alabama's EPP recognition status and exam requirements.
Whether an NC school music license needs any add-on beyond the base area.
Any transition timing or deadlines for the 6-month move, beyond the general LICN-025 exam timing.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer reaches the right needs_more_info verdict and covers the IPL/CPL thresholds, clear-license test, exam timing, and the 5114/162 score accurately with cited support. It omits the application and fee requirements and does not clearly flag that an existing NC CPL would make the out-of-state route inapplicable, which is the key premise correction.

question: Applicant with a BS in deaf education from Kentucky, wants to teach deaf students in NC. Which license?

answer.summary: The relevant teaching license area is Deaf and Hard of Hearing, and a bachelor's degree from an educator preparation program fits the teacher license level. Whether the applicant gets an Initial Professional License or a Continuing Professional License, and what exam steps apply, depends on whether the Kentucky program is recognized, the applicant's Kentucky license status, and years of licensed teaching experience.

claims.text: Deaf and Hard of Hearing is a listed Exceptional Children license area (Kindergarten through Grade 12) for teacher licenses in North Carolina.

To qualify for a teacher license, an applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the bachelor's level or higher, and a bachelor's degree is the A-Level. The applicant's BS therefore meets the degree level for a teacher license, provided the program qualifies.

An applicant is only eligible for a license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP. The applicant's highest EPP degree is the BS, so the license is at the bachelor's level.
An applicant who completed an EPP with a principal place of business outside North Carolina is an out-of-state applicant. A Kentucky program would fall in this category.
