question: teacher wants to sub in NC with an out-of-state license in biology, no NC license at all. allowed?

answer.summary: The policies provided do not say whether a substitute teacher must hold a North Carolina license, so I can't confirm that subbing without an NC license is allowed. The general rule is that a professional educator employed in an NC public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, an NC license, and an out-of-state biology license can lead to an NC initial professional license if the teacher qualifies.

claims.text: The general rule is that any person employed as a professional educator in a North Carolina public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, a professional educator license issued by DPI, except as otherwise provided by law.

A professional educator is an administrator, teacher, or student services personnel, and a teacher is an individual whose major responsibility is to teach or directly supervise teaching. The policies do not define substitute teaching or say whether a substitute is employed as a professional educator under this rule.

Service as a substitute teacher is not recognized for professional educator experience credit for salary purposes. This governs salary credit only and does not address whether a license is required to substitute.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an initial professional license by holding a license in the corresponding license area in another jurisdiction, or by completing an educator preparation program recognized by the jurisdiction where the program is located.

An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of experience who qualifies for an IPL in a license area other than Elementary or Special Education: General Curriculum must either pass an out-of-state exam for that area in the examining jurisdiction, or satisfy the NC exam requirements before or during the third year of licensure, having attempted the exam at least once during the first year.
The NC required test for Biology (license code 310) is Praxis 5236 with a required score of 154.

Under LICN-020, an applicant may qualify for an initial professional license by completing an EPP based outside North Carolina, or by holding a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction. An IPL entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

A PSU may request an IPL for an applicant under its employment only if the applicant has completed the requirements for a recognized NC EPP but has not met the exam requirements. This route does not fit a teacher whose preparation was out of state.

A PSU may request a permit to teach only for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other NC professional educator license. A permit is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

A PSU may request an emergency license only for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree with at least 18 relevant credit hours, has not completed a recognized EPP in that area, and does not qualify for a residency license. An emergency license is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be renewed.

question: Teacher is a CTE health science teacher with an active CPL, wants to add an EC area. Has 12 credits in special ed. Enough?

answer.summary: Twelve credit hours is not enough to add an Exceptional Children area through coursework, because LICN-013 requires 24 credit hours with a grade of C or better. If the area is Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, coursework cannot be used at all, so the teacher would need to pass the required licensure exam.

claims.text: A CPL holder may request to add a new license area to an existing CPL under LICN-013.

To add a teaching area by coursework, the applicant must complete 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area, with a grade of C or better in each course. The teacher's 12 credits fall short of this 24-hour requirement by 12 hours.
Exceptional Children: General Curriculum cannot be added through coursework alone. It may only be added by satisfying the applicable licensure examination requirements, regardless of credit hours.

The other route is to satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements for the area. For Special Education: General Curriculum, LICN-003 lists Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with a required score of 145, or Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with a required score of 233, plus a mathematics requirement (Pearson Test 203 or 7813 CKT Math). Other Exceptional Children areas have different required tests.

Exceptional Children areas are listed under LICN-010 §6(e), including General Curriculum, Adapted Curriculum, Learning Disabled, Cross Categorical, Severely/Profoundly Disabled, Mentally Disabled, Academically or Intellectually Gifted, Deaf and Hard of Hearing, Visually Impaired, and Behaviorally/Emotionally Disabled.

Did the teacher earn a grade of C or better in each of the 12 credits?

The policies do not state the fee for adding a license area, beyond the general fee table in LICN-008, which does not list a specific fee for adding an area by coursework or test.

It omits the CEU-to-semester-hour conversion and the CPL point, and it wrongly says the fee is not stated. Claim 2 cites only a heading that does not back the no-coursework assertion.

question: Applicant completed an EC program in NC in 2019 but never applied for a license. Now wants an RL. Still eligible?

answer.summary: The passages do not show a deadline that bars this applicant from a residency license because the 2019 program was completed years ago. Eligibility turns on whether the 2019 program was a recognized NC educator preparation program, whether the applicant has 24 credit hours in the target EC area or has passed the required exam, and whether a North Carolina PSU will request the license for them as an employee. The statutory requirement in G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) is not in the passages, so it must be checked separately.

claims.text: A PSU governing body or eligible nonpublic school may request a residency license only for an applicant under its employment, and the applicant must meet G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and have either 24 hours of coursework in the content area sought or passed the applicable licensure exam for that content area.
The passages do not state the text of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), so whether this applicant meets that subsection cannot be confirmed from the passages.
A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.

To qualify for a residency license based on coursework, the 24 hours must be in the content area for which the license is sought. For an EC applicant, the content area is one of the EC license areas listed in LICN-010, such as Exceptional Children: General Curriculum or Adapted Curriculum.

Under LICN-013, Exceptional Children: General Curriculum can only be added to a license by satisfying the licensure examination requirements, not through coursework alone. This applies to adding an area to an existing license, so it is relevant if the analyst is considering coursework-based eligibility for that area.

Licensure examination requirements for each EC license area are set out in LICN-003. For example, Special Education: General Curriculum requires the Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with a score of 145, plus alternatives listed in the table.

A teacher license requires completion of an educator preparation program at the applicable degree level. The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where it has its principal place of business.

An IPL requires completion of a recognized NC educator preparation program and EPP recommendation, which means the 2019 program must have been recognized for this route to apply to the applicant's history.

Applications must include official transcripts for degrees obtained and documentation that the applicant completed an EPP for the license classification sought, and the applicant must pay the application fee.

The passages do not state any time limit after which completed EPP coursework expires or stops counting toward a residency license. The only three-year EPP timeframe in the passages applies to servicemembers and spouses holding residency licenses who are called to active duty or relocated under military orders.
The passages do not contain a rule that an applicant who completed an EPP but never applied for a license is barred from later applying for a residency license.

question: Applicant has 2 yrs teaching in private school in NC, bachelor's in elem ed, wants RL. Does private school experience count?

answer.summary: Based on the passages, two years of private school teaching is not a listed requirement for a residency license. Eligibility turns on whether an eligible nonpublic school or public school unit requests the license for the applicant and whether the applicant has 24 hours of coursework in the content area or has passed the required exam. Private school experience may matter for salary experience credit, but only if it meets the full-time six-month rules and is not a one-teacher private school.

claims.text: A residency license may be requested by the governing body of a public school unit or an eligible nonpublic school for an applicant under its employment, if the applicant meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area for which the license is sought, or passed the applicable licensure examination requirements for that content area.

The passages define an 'eligible nonpublic school' only by reference to G.S. 115C-207.20(a)(5)a.2, which is not included in the passages, so whether this applicant's private school qualifies cannot be determined from the passages.

The residency license eligibility criteria in LICN-019 §1 do not mention prior years of teaching experience. The two years of private school teaching is therefore not a stated eligibility criterion for the residency license in these passages.

For salary experience credit, full-time work in a school unit of at least six calendar months within one fiscal year (July 1 through June 30) earns one year of experience credit. Two fiscal years of qualifying full-time work would earn two years of credit. Experience in a one-teacher private school is excluded from this credit.
The passages do not define 'school unit,' so whether this applicant's private school counts as a school unit for experience credit cannot be determined from the passages.
A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice.

To renew a residency license, the employing school must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program, is employed as a teacher in the public school unit or eligible nonpublic school, and acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year.

For Elementary (K-6), the required tests are Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with a score of 233, and Pearson Test 203 Mathematics Subtest or Praxis 7813 CKT Math Subtest with a score of 227 or 150.

answer.summary: The policies do not yet support a single license. A residency license may be requested only by the governing body of a public school unit (or eligible nonpublic school) for an applicant under its employment. The applicant must meet G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and have either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure examination for that content area. An out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for an IPL if the applicant holds a license in the corresponding license area in another jurisdiction, or completed an EPP recognized by the jurisdiction where that EPP is based. For an out-of-state IPL in a license area other than Elementary or Special Education: General Curriculum, the applicant must either pass an out-of-state exam for that area in the examining jurisdiction, or satisfy the NC licensure examination requirements before or during the third year, having attempted them at least once in the first year.

Band is not listed as its own area in the passages. Music is a Special Subject (K-12) license area, and its required licensure exam is Praxis 5114 with a required score of 162. Whether band maps to the Music area is not addressed in the passages.

question: Teacher has a master's in educational leadership and 4 years teaching. No admin license. Wants to be an assistant principal. Route?

answer.summary: Becoming an assistant principal requires either a principal license or a provisional assistant principal license, and the provisional license is governed by LICN-014 Section 7, which was not provided. A master's in educational leadership appears to meet the principal license degree-field requirement only if it came from an administrator preparation program, so the route depends on that fact and on the teacher's employment status.

claims.text: Any person employed as an assistant principal in a PSU must hold either a principal license or a provisional assistant principal license issued under LICN-014, Section 7.

A provisional assistant principal license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual employed as an assistant principal who meets LICN-014, Section 7. Because it is tied to current AP employment, the teacher would need an AP job offer to pursue it.
Assistant principals are classified as administrators under the policy series.
A principal license is a five-year renewable administrator license issued to an individual who meets LICN-011.

To qualify for a principal license (any administrator license other than superintendent or Exceptional Children program administrator), the applicant must have completed an administrator preparation program (APP) at the master's, specialist, or doctoral level.

An APP is a program approved by the State Board of Education to prepare, train, and recommend candidates for administrator licensure. Completing a master's in educational leadership alone does not establish APP completion; the teacher must confirm the program was an approved APP.

For a principal license, the master's degree must be in School Administration, Educational Leadership, or another education-related field. An educational leadership master's meets the field requirement on its face.
An applicant is eligible only at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP or APP. The teacher's master's would be the qualifying level if it was completed through an APP.

question: What's the difference between an IPL and a CPL in NC?

answer.summary: An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license, while a CPL is a five-year, renewable license. Both allow independent practice in NC, but a CPL requires more qualifications, including at least three years of licensed teaching experience and completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

claims.text: An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license issued to an applicant or professional educator who meets the relevant requirements set by SBE policy.
A CPL is a five-year, renewable license issued to an applicant or professional educator who meets the relevant requirements set by SBE policy.
Both an IPL and a CPL entitle the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

To qualify for an IPL, an applicant must have completed a recognized NC educator preparation program and be recommended by the EPP, or have completed an EPP based outside NC, or hold a clear out-of-state license and have fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

To qualify for a teacher CPL, an applicant must hold an NC IPL or residency license, satisfy the applicable licensure exam requirements before or during the third year of licensure, have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and have completed a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless the applicant has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside NC or previously held a CPL that reverted to an IPL.
An out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an IPL to a CPL.
A CPL must be renewed every five years, and teachers must complete eight CEUs in each renewal cycle, with a rating of at least proficient on the most recent annual evaluation.

If a teacher on a CPL is placed on a mandatory improvement plan by the employing LSAU, DPI issues the teacher an IPL, which has a three-year term; at the end of that term, the teacher may apply for a CPL if the requirements are met.
The reversion of a teacher's license from a CPL to an IPL shall not be construed as a demotion or result in a reduction of salary.
The fee to recommend converting an initial license to a continuing professional license, when opened by the employing school system, is $60.

not_covered: What happens to an IPL at the end of its three-year term if the holder has not converted it to a CPL.
Whether the IPL in the LICN-030 mandatory improvement plan context applies to non-teacher license classifications.
Salary or pay differences between IPL and CPL holders.

metrics.judge_rationale: The answer gets the core difference right (three-year nonrenewable IPL versus five-year renewable CPL), the shared practice entitlement, the teacher CPL requirements, the out-of-state exam restriction, and the mandatory improvement plan reversion, and every claim is backed by its cited text. It omits peripheral details such as the PSU exam-deferred IPL route, administrator and student services CPL requirements, and renewal specifics for those roles.

answer.summary: Under the current policies, a candidate with no bachelor's degree does not qualify for an NC Emergency License, so the math EL granted last year conflicts with current rules and should be checked before anything else. The English CPL is not eligible to be treated as lapsed on its face, since a CPL runs a five-year renewal cycle, so its status depends on the actual expiration date, renewal or validation paperwork, employment history, CEUs, and evaluation rating.

To receive an Emergency License, the applicant must hold at least a bachelor's degree that includes at least 18 credit hours of coursework relevant to the licensure area, must not have completed a recognized EPP in that area, and must not qualify for a residency license.

A candidate with no degree does not meet the bachelor's degree requirement for an Emergency License in math under the current policy, so the policies do not support the EL the analyst describes. The policies provided cannot confirm which rules applied when the EL was granted last year; the current versions are effective 2026-07-01.

The only teaching license areas that may be issued to an applicant with a high school diploma or associate's degree are Career and Technical Education, JROTC, and Safety and Driver Education. Math is not on that list.
A Permit to Teach also requires at least a bachelor's degree, so a candidate with no degree would not qualify for that route either under the current policy.
A CPL is a five-year renewable license, and renewal is required every five years. The renewal cycle is the five-year period between renewals of a CPL.

Because a CPL runs for five years, a CPL that is three years old would not, on the passages alone, be due for renewal yet. The passages do not state when a particular CPL expires, so whether it has actually lapsed cannot be determined from the facts given. Under the general rule, a license expires June 30 of the calendar year it is set to expire unless renewed, extended, or converted.

Renewing a teacher CPL requires eight CEUs per cycle: for Grades 6-12, four in the license area and four general CEUs; for Pre-K-5, three in the license area, three literacy CEUs, and two general CEUs. One CEU equals either two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours of professional development.

A teacher employed by a local board must have a rating of at least Proficient on the most recent annual evaluation to renew a CPL. Proficient means a Proficient or higher rating on three of five standards, including Standard 4.

If an expired CPL is not renewed and the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year, a PSU may request that DPI validate it, even without the requisite CEUs. A validated CPL is effective for three years, and the educator must then complete the renewal requirements by the end of the third year to renew for a new five-year cycle.

A teacher who is employed, not deemed proficient, and in the final year of a renewal cycle may be placed on a mandatory improvement plan by the LSAU. If so and the teacher otherwise meets requirements, DPI issues an IPL, and the teacher may apply for a CPL after the three-year IPL term.

question: What's the difference between a Residency License and an Initial Professional License?

answer.summary: A Residency License is a one-year license, renewable twice, for someone who is enrolled in an educator preparation program (EPP) and teaching in a PSU, and it can be requested only if the applicant has 24 hours of content coursework or has passed the required exam. An Initial Professional License (IPL) is a three-year, nonrenewable license for an applicant who has completed an EPP (or meets the out-of-state option) and has the EPP recommendation, though a PSU can request an IPL for someone who has finished EPP requirements but not the exams. Both can later convert to a Continuing Professional License (CPL) under LICN-024.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.
An IPL is a three-year, nonrenewable license issued to an applicant or professional educator who meets the relevant SBE policy requirements.

A residency license may be requested by a PSU governing body for an applicant who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area, or passed the applicable licensure examination for that content area.

To qualify for an IPL, an applicant must either have completed a recognized NC educator preparation program and be recommended by the EPP; have completed an EPP based outside NC; or hold a clear out-of-state license and have fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

A PSU may request an IPL for an applicant who has completed all academic, field, clinical, and other requirements for a recognized NC EPP but has not satisfied the licensure examination requirements. In that case, the EPP recommendation is not required.

To renew a residency license, the employing PSU must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized EPP, is employed as a teacher in the PSU, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year of the license.

If a residency license is not renewed for the second or third year, it expires. The PSU may ask DPI to reinstate it if it hires the applicant within three years of the initial residency license's effective date, provided it has not already been renewed twice.

To convert a residency license to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL requirements in LICN-020 or the CPL requirements in LICN-024 and be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee. If these are met by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL takes effect July 1 of the next fiscal year.
An IPL entitles the licensee to practice as an independent professional educator in North Carolina.

A PSU employing a residency license holder must provide at least three hours of field experience before the teacher begins classroom teaching, and at least 10 hours of field experience over the first year.
An IPL may be converted to a clear CPL if the required state exam is taken at least once during the first year of the license and passed before or during the third year.

Under LICN-024, a CPL requires holding an NC initial professional or residency license, satisfying exam requirements, having at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completing a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.
A person who holds or previously held a residency license is not eligible for a permit to teach or an emergency license in the same license area.

The passages do not specify whether residency and IPL holders are paid differently on the State Salary Schedule.

The passages do not say whether an IPL holder must complete the field experience or professional development required of residency holders.

question: Is there still a Permit to Teach in NC, and who is it for?

answer.summary: Yes, the Permit to Teach is still in the adopted policies (LICN-017, effective 2026-07-01). A public school unit's governing body may request one for an employee who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license, and it is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year requested, with no extension or renewal.

The applicant must also have never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license to qualify for a Permit to Teach.
A Permit to Teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested, and it cannot be extended or renewed.

For State Salary Schedule pay, a Permit to Teach is issued at the same level as a bachelor's degree (A-Level) teacher license with zero years of experience, regardless of the applicant's education level or prior work experience.
Add-on license areas cannot be added to a Permit to Teach.

question: Can you list the license types NCDPI issues to classroom teachers?

answer.summary: LICN-010 lists nine teacher license classifications: Initial Professional, Continuing Professional, Residency, Limited, Permit to Teach, Emergency, International Faculty, Lifetime, and Provisional. The policies provided do not describe the Provisional License because its governing policy, LICN-014, is not among them.

An Initial Professional License is a three-year, nonrenewable license.
A Continuing Professional License is a five-year, renewable license.
A Residency License is a one-year license, renewable twice.
A Limited License is a three-year renewable license issued to an individual who has completed an EPP but has not satisfied the applicable licensure examination requirements.

A Permit to Teach is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed. A PSU governing body may request one for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other NC professional educator license.
An Emergency License is a one-year nonrenewable license. It is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed.

An International Faculty License cannot be renewed but may be extended for two years at the request of the sponsor and employing PSU. It is available to J-1 visa holders who do not meet the requirements for any other DPI license.

A Lifetime License requires no renewal. It can be obtained by converting a current CPL if the applicant has 30 or more years of creditable NCTSERS service or 30 or more years of combined NC licensed experience.

The Provisional License is listed as a teacher license classification and references LICN-014, Section 7, but LICN-014 is not in the provided passages. LICN-001 §2(u) defines only a provisional assistant principal license, which is an administrator credential.

question: What does an Emergency License allow someone to do that a Permit to Teach doesn't?

answer.summary: The main practical difference is pay: an Emergency License holder may qualify for graduate degree pay or experience pay under LICN-006, while a Permit to Teach holder is placed at the zero-experience A-level regardless of education or experience. The Emergency License also requires qualifications the Permit does not (18 relevant credit hours and no residency eligibility), and the passages do not describe any difference in the teaching duties the two licenses allow.

claims.text: A Permit to Teach may be requested by a PSU governing body for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license.

An Emergency License may be requested by a PSU governing body for an applicant who holds a bachelor's degree with at least 18 credit hours of coursework relevant to the licensure area, has not completed a recognized educator preparation program in that area, and does not qualify for a residency license.
A Permit to Teach and an Emergency License are both valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which they were requested, and neither can be extended or renewed.

For State Salary Schedule pay, a Permit to Teach is issued at the same level as a bachelor's degree (A-Level) teacher with zero years of experience, regardless of the applicant's education level or prior work experience.
For State Salary Schedule pay, an Emergency License is issued at the A-Level, but the applicant may qualify for graduate degree pay or experience pay under LICN-006.

Under LICN-006, experience credit can be awarded for full-time school work of at least six calendar months in a fiscal year, and graduate salary pay can be authorized for a master's or higher degree that meets the listed criteria, including being directly related to the license area or assignment.
A person who holds or previously held a residency license is not eligible for an Emergency License in the same license area.

The policies provided describe a teacher license as entitling the licensee to teach in the license area(s) indicated on the license, but they do not state any different teaching scope for a Permit to Teach versus an Emergency License.

question: Is there a Limited License for teachers, and when is it used?

answer.summary: Yes, a Limited License is a teacher license classification in North Carolina. It is used when a PSU employs an applicant who has completed an educator preparation program but has not yet met the licensure examination requirements, and it is available only for teaching license areas. Whether it applies to a specific educator depends on the facts listed in the questions below.

claims.text: A Limited License is one of the teacher license classifications DPI may issue.
A Limited License is defined as a three-year renewable license issued to an individual who has completed an EPP but has not satisfied the applicable licensure examination requirements.

A PSU governing body may request a Limited License for an applicant under its employment if the applicant meets the requirements of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(4a). A Limited License may only be issued for teaching license areas, not for administrator or student services personnel license areas.

A person who previously held a lateral entry license under G.S. 115C-297 (repealed by S.L. 2017-189) can also qualify for a Limited License if the person satisfies all IPL or CPL requirements except the licensure examination requirements, is currently employed by the PSU governing body, and the PSU submits an affidavit signed by the local superintendent (or equivalent) and the school principal stating the person is employed, is an effective teacher, and will be encouraged to pursue an IPL or CPL.

To renew a Limited License, the employing PSU must submit an affidavit signed by the supervising principal and local superintendent attesting the licensee is currently employed, is an effective teacher, and that the PSU will encourage the licensee to pursue a CPL.

To renew a Limited License, the licensee must meet or exceed expected EVAAS growth where data is available. If there is more than one year of data, DPI averages it. Data is limited to years since the license was first issued or last renewed, and DPI does not consider 2019-2020 or 2020-2021 EVAAS data.
A Limited License is not portable. Except for servicemembers and spouses covered by LICN-028, it cannot be transferred from one PSU to another.

A servicemember or spouse holding a Limited License who relocates within North Carolina under military orders and takes a job with a different local board of education keeps the license valid for the new assignment.
Additional teaching license areas cannot be added to a Limited License.
A Limited License is a teaching license only. Administrator and student services personnel licenses are not issued as Limited Licenses.

The provided passages do not describe the process for converting a Limited License to an IPL or CPL.

question: How long is a Residency License valid and can it be extended?

answer.summary: A Residency License is valid for one year and can be renewed twice, for a maximum of three years. Each renewal requires the employing school unit to document enrollment in an educator preparation program, employment as a teacher, and at least six months of teaching experience in the preceding school year, and 10 days of professional development must be completed in the first year.

claims.text: A residency license is a one-year license, renewable twice, issued to an individual who meets the qualifications of LICN-019.

Renewing a residency license requires the employing PSU governing body or eligible nonpublic school to document to DPI that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program, is employed as a teacher in that school unit, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year of the residency license.

If an applicant fails to renew a residency license for the second or third year, the license expires. A PSU or eligible nonpublic school that hires the applicant within three years of the initial residency license's effective date may ask DPI to reinstate it, provided the license has not already been renewed twice and the applicant is employed by that PSU and enrolled in a recognized EPP.

To convert a residency license to an IPL or CPL, the applicant must meet the IPL requirements in LICN-020 or the CPL requirements in LICN-024 and be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee. If these are met by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL or CPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year; otherwise the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL is effective when the requirements are met.

The policies use the term "renew" for residency licenses. They do not describe an "extension" of a residency license, and I found no provision allowing a residency license to be extended beyond the two renewals.

question: What are the requirements for a CPL in terms of years of experience and renewal cycle?

answer.summary: For a teacher, a CPL requires at least three years of licensed teaching experience, completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies, and a North Carolina IPL or residency license plus the required exams. A CPL is renewed on a five-year renewal cycle, and teachers must also complete 8 CEUs per cycle and meet evaluation requirements. The passages give no years-of-experience requirement for administrator or student services CPLs, so tell me the license type if you need that detail.

claims.text: To qualify for a continuing professional teacher license, an applicant must hold an initial professional educator license or residency license in North Carolina.
A teacher CPL applicant must have at least three years of licensed teaching experience.

A teacher CPL applicant must satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, and must attempt the exams at least once during the first year of licensure if the exams were not passed before receiving an IPL.

A teacher CPL applicant must complete a Beginning Teacher Support Program under TCED-016, unless the applicant has at least three years of licensed teaching experience outside North Carolina, or previously held a CPL that reverted to an IPL under LICN-030.
The renewal cycle is the five-year period between each renewal of a CPL.
Each teacher holding a CPL must renew that license every five years.
Each person holding an administrator license must renew that license every five years.
Each person holding a student services personnel license must renew that license every five years.

For a teacher in Grades 6 through 12, renewal requires eight CEUs per cycle: four in the license area and four general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment. Teachers in Pre-Kindergarten through Grade 5 must complete eight CEUs with a different breakdown.
One CEU equals either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from an institution of higher education, or ten clock hours of professional development programming.
Teachers employed by a local board of education must have a rating of at least proficient on the most recent annual evaluation to renew a CPL, including a Proficient rating on Standard 4.

A continuing professional administrator or student services personnel license requires satisfying the applicable licensure exam requirements (before or during the third year, with an attempt in the first year if not passed before the IPL) and meeting the other requirements of LICN-011 or LICN-012. The passages state no years-of-experience requirement for these license types.

An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a CPL based on a clear out-of-state license and either National Board certification or substantially similar licensure requirements.

question: How many CEUs are needed to renew a CPL, and do any have to be in a specific area?

answer.summary: A teacher renewing a CPL needs 8 CEUs per five-year cycle. Whether any must be in a specific area depends on the teacher's grade band (Pre-K to 5 or 6 to 12), and administrators and student services personnel follow different rules. Please confirm the license type and grade band before giving a final answer.

claims.text: Each CPL must be renewed every five years, and the renewal cycle is the five-year period between renewals of a CPL.
A CEU is credit for renewing a license. One CEU equals either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from an institution of higher education, or ten clock hours of professional development programming.

For a teacher in Pre-Kindergarten through Grade 5, the renewal cycle requires 8 CEUs: 3 in the teacher's license area (aligned with Standards 3 and 4 of the NC Professional Teaching Standards), 3 related to literacy, and 2 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment. Arithmetic: 3 + 3 + 2 = 8. So 3 of the 8 must be in the license area and 3 must be literacy-related.

For a teacher in Grades 6 through 12, the renewal cycle requires 8 CEUs: 4 in the teacher's license area (aligned with Standards 3 and 4 of the NC Professional Teaching Standards) and 4 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment. Arithmetic: 4 + 4 = 8. So 4 of the 8 must be in the license area and no literacy-specific CEUs are required.

Because the CEU definition is ten clock hours or two-thirds of a semester hour, 8 CEUs equal 80 clock hours or 5.33 semester hours (8 x 2/3). The policies do not state which form a teacher must use, so this is a conversion from the definition only.

For an administrator, the renewal cycle requires 8 CEUs: 4 focused on the administrator's leadership role in instruction, human resources, and management, and 4 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment. So 4 must be in the leadership-focus area.

For student services personnel, the renewal cycle requires 8 CEUs: 4 that align with the NC standards for the relevant professional discipline under the EVAL policy series, and 4 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment. So 4 must align with the discipline standards.

A teacher who earns National Board Certification in a renewal cycle receives credit for all 8 CEUs for that cycle. A teacher who renews National Board Certification receives credit for 2 CEUs for that cycle.

Hours spent in mandatory training programs count toward CEUs if the training is required by State law or by a local board as a condition of employment, and the educator has otherwise met the renewal requirements for the license type.
A PSU may require continuing education beyond the State requirements based on local needs.

question: What's the process to move from an RL to an IPL?

answer.summary: To convert a residency license (RL) to an initial professional license (IPL), the holder must meet the IPL requirements in LICN-020 and be recommended by the educator preparation program (EPP) that prepared them. If those requirements are met by June 30 of the RL's third year, the IPL takes effect July 1 of the next fiscal year; if not, the RL expires and the IPL takes effect when the requirements are met. Eligibility depends on the holder's EPP and preparation history, which you have not provided.

claims.text: To convert a residency license to an IPL, the applicant must meet the IPL requirements in LICN-020 and be recommended by the EPP that prepared the licensee.

Under LICN-020, an applicant qualifies for an IPL by (a) completing a recognized North Carolina EPP and being recommended by that EPP for the requested license, (b) completing an EPP based outside North Carolina, or (c) holding a clear out-of-state license and having fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

Timing: if the applicant satisfies the requirements by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, the IPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires and the IPL is effective on the date the requirements are satisfied.

To keep the residency license in renewal, the PSU must document that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized EPP, is employed as a teacher in the PSU, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year of the residency license.

A residency license may be converted to a Continuing Professional License instead of an IPL, but that requires meeting the CPL requirements in LICN-024, including passing licensure exams before or during the third year, at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completing a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.
A complete license application requires the documents listed in LICN-004 and payment of the fee set in LICN-008.

If the applicant is a servicemember or military spouse whose residency license timeframe is affected by military orders, the three-year timeframe for completing an EPP and other requirements for an IPL or CPL is held in abeyance until the servicemember returns to North Carolina and resumes employment in a North Carolina public school.

question: How does reinstatement work for a license that expired a few years ago?

answer.summary: The passages do not use 'reinstatement' for an expired license. Reinstatement under LICN-007 applies to revoked or denied licenses, while an expired CPL is generally handled by a PSU requesting validation under LICN-033, which depends on whether the educator was employed by any PSU in the preceding fiscal year and on the license type. Please confirm whether the license was revoked or only expired, the license type, and the educator's employment since expiration.

claims.text: Under LICN-001 section 3(g), every license expires on June 30 of the calendar year in which it is set to expire, unless renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy.

LICN-007 section 8(a) allows an individual whose license has been revoked, or whose application has been denied, to petition for reinstatement or reconsideration no sooner than 12 months after the effective date of the revocation or denial. This pathway is written for revoked or denied licenses, not licenses that simply expired.

Under LICN-007 section 8(b) and (c), the petition must be in writing to the Superintendent and explain why the circumstances no longer justify prohibiting the petitioner from holding a license. The Superintendent may deny, grant, or grant on probation, and a probationary grant is reviewed one year later.

For an expired continuing professional license, the governing body of a PSU may ask DPI to validate the expired CPL for an applicant under its employment, even if the educator does not have the required CEUs, provided the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year.

A validated CPL is effective for three years. To renew it for a new five-year cycle, the educator must complete the relevant renewal requirements in LICN-030, LICN-031, or LICN-032 by the end of the third year.
The fee for a PSU to open a Validate an Expired Continuing Professional License request is $60, listed under applications opened by the employing school system on behalf of educators.

For a teacher whose CPL expired at the end of a renewal cycle without being placed on a mandatory improvement plan, the teacher may apply for an IPL 30 days after receiving DPI's notice of expiration.

A teacher's mandatory improvement plan under LICN-030 section 2(b) is available only to a teacher employed by a local board of education who holds a current CPL, is in the final year of a renewal cycle, and was not deemed proficient. If placed on the plan and otherwise qualified, DPI issues an IPL.

question: What's the renewal deadline for a standard CPL, and what happens if it lapses?

question: How do you add a new licensure area to an existing NC license?

answer.summary: A teacher can add a new license area to an existing initial professional license (IPL) or continuing professional license (CPL) either by passing the required licensure exam for that area or by completing 24 credit hours of coursework in the area with a grade of C or better in each course. Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum can be added only by passing the exam, and licenses such as permits, emergency, residency, limited, provisional, and international faculty cannot receive added areas under LICN-013.

claims.text: An applicant may request to add a new license area to an existing IPL or CPL.
An applicant may add a license area to an IPL only if the applicant has already met the licensure examination requirements for the initial license area.

To add an area to a teaching license, the applicant must either satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements for that license area, or complete 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area and obtain a grade of C or better in each course.
For Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, the area can be added only by satisfying the licensure examination requirements; coursework alone is not an option.

DPI shall not add teaching areas under the add-on rule to a Permit to Teach, Emergency License, Residency License, Limited License, Provisional License, International Faculty License, or Career and Technical Education Restricted License.

The 24 credit hours in the coursework route must come from an institution of higher education and be in the license area. The policies do not define whether these must be semester hours, so the analyst should confirm the unit with DPI.

An out-of-state applicant who qualifies for a teacher license under LICN-025 Sections 1 or 2 may add a teaching area based solely on a passing score on an out-of-state exam in that area, provided the exam results are submitted with the initial North Carolina application.
If an out-of-state applicant wants to add an area after the North Carolina license has been issued, the applicant must follow the LICN-013 requirements.
Adding a license area is a licensure service with an individual-educator fee of $60 for the test or 24 semester hours route.
citations: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

claims.text: A complete application must be submitted, including the application fee, for licensure services in LICN-008; DPI issues a license once the application is complete.

For licensure services other than renewal, a complete application must reach DPI by April 15 of a fiscal year to guarantee processing before fiscal year end. Later applications that DPI does not approve before fiscal year end cannot be paid with State or federal funds for that fiscal year.
The fee schedule also lists an 'Add Area by Program Completion' option at $60, but the LICN-013 policy text does not describe that route.
citations: LICN-008 (North Carolina Department of Public Instruction Licensure Fees)

question: What are the testing requirements for adding a licensure area?

answer.summary: An applicant can add a license area either by passing that area's required licensure exam or by completing 24 semester credit hours of coursework in the area with a grade of C or better in each course. Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum can be added only by passing the exam, and the license type held also limits what can be added.

claims.text: To add a teaching license area, an applicant must either satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements for that area, or complete 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the license area with a grade of C or better in each course.

Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum can be added only by satisfying the applicable licensure examination requirements. Coursework alone does not work for these two areas.
An applicant may add a license area to an Initial Professional License only if the applicant has already met the licensure examination requirements for the initial license area.

The required exam and minimum score for each area are listed in the NCSBE approved testing table, which gives a Praxis test code and required score by area of licensure. The table also includes non-Praxis exams such as ACTFL OPI and WPT, Pearson tests, and the NCBOESLPA requirements for some areas.

Testing timing for licenses generally requires the exam to be attempted at least once during the first year of licensure and passed before or during the third year. This is stated for administrator and student services licenses, and the teacher CPL rules are similar.

A Permit to Teach, Emergency License, Residency License, Limited License, Provisional License, International Faculty License, and Career and Technical Education Restricted License cannot have teaching areas added under the add-on rule.

An out-of-state applicant may add a teaching area at initial application based solely on a passing score on an out-of-state exam in that area, if evidence of the results is submitted. If the applicant adds the area after receiving a North Carolina license, LICN-013 applies.

question: Can a teacher teach a course outside their licensure area, and is there a time limit?

answer.summary: The policies provided do not say whether a teacher may teach a course outside their licensure area, and they set no time limit for doing so. They do say a teacher license authorizes teaching in the license areas listed on it, and they explain how an area can be added to an IPL or CPL, which may be the practical route to cover a course.

claims.text: A teacher license entitles the licensee to teach in the license area(s) indicated on the license.
Any person employed as a professional educator in a North Carolina public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, a professional educator license issued by DPI.
The policies provided contain no rule permitting or prohibiting teaching outside a licensed area, and no time limit for doing so.

An applicant may add a new license area to an existing IPL or CPL. An IPL can add an area only if the applicant has met the licensure examination requirements for the initial area. To add an area, the applicant must either satisfy the applicable licensure examination requirements for that area or complete 24 credit hours of higher-education coursework in the area with a grade of C or better in each course.
Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum can be added only by satisfying the licensure examination requirements, not through coursework alone.

A Permit to Teach, Emergency License, Residency License, Limited License, Provisional License, International Faculty License, or CTE Restricted License cannot have teaching areas added under LICN-013 §1.
A Permit to Teach and an Emergency License are each valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which they were requested, and neither can be extended or renewed.

A residency license may be requested for an additional license area if the applicant holds a clear license in another area and meets the requirements of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) for each requested area.

question: What's the Birth through Kindergarten license and who qualifies for it?

answer.summary: Birth through Kindergarten is a teacher license area under the Elementary classification, with licensure code 14 and no required licensure exam. The policies provided do not set any Birth-K-specific qualifications, so the general teacher license requirements apply: completion of an educator preparation program at the bachelor's level or higher, with the license issued as an initial or continuing professional license.

An applicant is only eligible for a license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP.

Applicants with only a high school diploma or associate's degree may be licensed only in Career and Technical Education, JROTC, and Safety and Driver Education, so that alternative path does not extend to Birth through Kindergarten.
The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business.

A teacher license is classified as an Initial Professional License, Continuing Professional License, Residency License, Limited License, Permit to Teach, Emergency License, International Faculty License, Lifetime License, or Provisional License, depending on the applicant's qualifications.

An applicant qualifies for an Initial Professional License by completing a recognized NC educator preparation program and being recommended by the EPP, by completing an out-of-state EPP, or by holding an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

A Continuing Professional License for teachers requires an initial or residency license in North Carolina, satisfaction of applicable examination requirements (none apply to this area per the testing table), at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

question: Is a school social worker license issued by NCDPI or by another agency?

answer.summary: Based on the provided policies, a school social worker license is issued by the Department of Public Instruction (DPI), as a classification of the student services personnel license. The only other licensing body named in these policies, the NCBOESLPA, applies to audiologists and speech-language pathologists, not school social workers.

claims.text: DPI issues professional educator licenses in three classifications: Teacher, Administrator, and Student Services Personnel.
School social work is included within the definition of student services personnel.
School social worker is one of the classifications of the student services personnel license, and the license is governed by LICN-012.
A school social worker license requires preparation at the bachelor's degree level (A-Level) or higher.
The NCBOESLPA license requirement applies to school audiologists and school speech-language pathologists, not to school social workers.
The student services personnel license is a 5-year renewable license issued to an individual who meets the requirements of LICN-012.

question: What license does a school counselor need in NC, and what's the degree requirement?

answer.summary: A school counselor in NC holds a Student Services Personnel License classified as School Counselor. To qualify, the applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the master's, specialist, or doctoral level, and the license is issued only at the highest EPP degree level completed. Licensure examination requirements also apply, and the School Counselor test entry in the LICN-003 table appears malformed and should be checked against the source.

claims.text: School counseling is classified as student services personnel.
A student services personnel license is a 5-year renewable license issued to an individual who meets the requirements of LICN-012.
School Counselor is one of the classifications of student services personnel license.

To qualify for a student services personnel license, including School Counselor, an applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the Master's (M-Level), Specialist (S-Level), or Doctoral (D-Level) degree level.
An applicant is only eligible for a license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP. The applicant may still qualify for graduate salary pay under LICN-006.
The degree level printed on a license is based on the highest degree issued to the applicant by an educator preparation program.

Applicants for a student services personnel license must satisfy any applicable licensure examination requirements before or during the third year of licensure, and must attempt the examinations at least once during the first year of licensure.

If the applicant satisfies the examination requirements before initial application, DPI issues a continuing professional license. If not, but the applicant otherwise meets the qualifications, DPI issues an initial professional license.

The LICN-003 testing table lists School Counselor (code 005) with a required test entry shown as '5 422' and a required score of 159. The entry's formatting is irregular, so the exact test number should be confirmed against the official table.

question: Is there a CTE license that doesn't require a bachelor's degree?

answer.summary: Yes, under LICN-010 an applicant with only a high school diploma (or equivalent) or an associate's degree may be issued a teaching license in Career and Technical Education, but only if the applicant meets all other requirements for the license classification sought. The analyst should confirm the license classification, the applicant's education and exam status, and the separate CTE manual the policies reference, which was not provided.

claims.text: The general rule for a teacher license is that the applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the bachelor's level or higher (A-Level, M-Level, S-Level, or D-Level), except as provided in Section 5 of LICN-010.

An applicant with a high school diploma (or equivalent) or an associate's degree (V-Level) may be issued a teaching license in Career and Technical Education, provided the applicant meets all other requirements for the license classification sought, as provided in Section 5.

The degree exception in LICN-010 §4 does not waive other requirements. Each teacher license must be classified as an IPL, CPL, Residency, Limited, Permit, Emergency, International Faculty, Lifetime, or Provisional license, and each of those classifications has its own qualification rules.

Under the IPL rule, a North Carolina applicant must have completed a recognized educator preparation program and be recommended by the EPP, or have completed an EPP based outside North Carolina, or hold a clear out-of-state license and have fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience there. The passages do not state how this EPP requirement applies to the high school diploma or associate's degree route for CTE.

Career and Technical Education license areas include Agriculture Education, Aviation Education, Business/Finance/IT Education, Family and Consumer Sciences, Health Sciences Education, Marketing Education, Technology/Engineering/Design Education, and Trade and Industrial Education (including Welding, Construction, and Public Safety), among others.
Permits to Teach and Emergency Licenses both require at least a bachelor's degree, so they are not a route for a CTE applicant without a bachelor's degree.
CTE licensure testing is governed in part by the CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual, which LICN-003 refers to but which is not among the passages provided.

question: What's the license for a school media coordinator, and what's the difference from a media specialist?

answer.summary: Under the provided policies, a school media coordinator holds a Student Services Personnel license in the Media Coordinator classification, which requires an educator preparation program at the master's, specialist, or doctoral level and the Praxis 5312 with a score of 154 (test code 076). The policies do not mention a 'media specialist' license, so I cannot state how the two differ.

claims.text: Media Coordinator is one of the classifications of the student services personnel license.
Student services personnel include individuals employed in media coordination.
A student services personnel license is a 5-year renewable license issued to an individual who meets the requirements of LICN-012.

To qualify for a student services personnel license, including Media Coordinator, an applicant must have completed an educator preparation program at the master's (M-Level), specialist (S-Level), or doctoral (D-Level) degree level.
An applicant is only eligible for a license at the highest degree level at which the applicant completed an EPP.
The licensure exam for Media Coordinator is Praxis test 5312 with a required score of 154 (licensure code 076).

The applicant must satisfy the licensure exam requirement before or during the third year of licensure, and must attempt it at least once during the first year. If the exam is passed before initial application, DPI issues a continuing professional license; otherwise DPI issues an initial professional license.

Renewal of a student services personnel license occurs every five years and requires eight CEUs per renewal cycle: four CEUs aligned with the North Carolina standards for the relevant professional discipline (EVAL policy series) and four general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment.
One CEU equals either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from an institution of higher education or ten clock hours of professional development programming.
Media Supervisor (code 078, Praxis 5412, score 146) is listed separately under Administrative/Supervisory areas, not under student services personnel.

question: What license do you need to teach Exceptional Children in NC?

answer.summary: The policies do not name one license for teaching Exceptional Children. The required license depends on the educator's degree level, whether they completed an NC-recognized educator preparation program in an EC area, their testing status, and whether they are out-of-state or already hold an NC license. Ask the questions listed below before choosing a classification.

claims.text: Individuals employed as a professional educator in an NC public school must hold, or be qualified to hold, a professional educator license issued by DPI under SBE policy.

Exceptional Children is a teacher license category. Its license areas include Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, Exceptional Children: Adapted Curriculum, Learning Disabled, Cross Categorical (Mildly/Moderately Disabled), Severely/Profoundly Disabled, Mentally Disabled, Academically or Intellectually Gifted, Deaf and Hard of Hearing, Visually Impaired, and Behaviorally/Emotionally Disabled (K-12).
A teacher license entitles the licensee to teach in the license area(s) indicated on the license, so the EC area must appear on the license.

To qualify for a teacher license, an applicant must complete an educator preparation program at the Bachelor's (A), Master's (M), Specialist (S), or Doctoral (D) level, with exceptions in Section 5. The applicant is licensed only at the highest degree level at which they completed an EPP, though they may qualify for graduate salary pay under LICN-006.

Each teacher license is classified as an Initial Professional License (LICN-020), Continuing Professional License (LICN-024), Residency License (LICN-019), Limited License (LICN-023), Permit to Teach (LICN-017), Emergency License (LICN-018), International Faculty License (LICN-026), Lifetime License (LICN-027), or Provisional License (LICN-014), based on the applicant's qualifications.

An IPL is available to an applicant who completed a recognized NC EPP and is recommended by the EPP, to an applicant who completed an EPP based outside NC, or to an applicant holding a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience there.
A PSU may request an IPL for an applicant who completed all NC EPP requirements but has not satisfied the licensure examination requirements, and the EPP recommendation is not required in that case.

A CPL for teachers requires an IPL or residency license in NC, satisfying the applicable exam requirements before or during the third year of licensure, at least three years of licensed teaching experience, and completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.

Licensure examination requirements for EC areas are listed in the LICN-003 table. Special Education: General Curriculum (88091) lists Foundational Knowledge Test 5355 with score 145, and also lists Pearson Test 890 Foundations of Reading with score 233 and a mathematics option (Pearson Test 203 or 7813 CKT Math). Special Education: Adapted Curriculum (88092) requires Tests 5547 (score 156) and 5511 (score 148). Cross Categorical (88001) requires 5355 (145) and 5511 (148).

Academically or Intellectually Gifted requires no test if earned through a recognized EPP. Otherwise, the applicant may add the area by passing Praxis Gifted Education test 5358 with a minimum score of 157.

An out-of-state applicant who qualifies for an IPL in Special Education: General Curriculum must satisfy NC examination requirements by the end of the third year of licensure, regardless of whether an out-of-state exam was passed.

A Residency License may be requested for an applicant who meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either completed at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passed the applicable licensure exam. This classification is a one-year license, renewable twice, under LICN-001 §2(w) and LICN-019.

A Permit to Teach may be requested only for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other NC professional educator license. It is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be renewed.

An Emergency License requires at least a bachelor's degree with at least 18 credit hours relevant to the area, no completed recognized EPP in that area, and no qualification for a residency license. It is valid until June 30 and cannot be renewed.

A Limited License may be requested for a teaching license area if the applicant meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(4a). It is a three-year renewable license and is not portable between PSUs, except for servicemembers and spouses under LICN-028.

A teacher may add an EC area to an existing IPL or CPL by satisfying the exam requirements for that area or by completing 24 credit hours of coursework in the area with a grade of C or better in each course. Exceptional Children: General Curriculum cannot be added through coursework alone.

Teachers in the residency, emergency, or permit classifications may not hold a second license of the same type in the same area. A person who holds or previously held a residency license is not eligible for a permit to teach or emergency license in that area.

question: What's required for a Career and Technical Education license in NC?

answer.summary: Career and Technical Education (CTE) is a teacher license area, not a separate license type, so the basic requirements follow the teacher license rules. Applicants with only a high school diploma or associate's degree can be issued a CTE teaching license if they meet the other requirements for their license classification, and five CTE areas have listed licensure tests. The passages do not include the CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual, so the Class V, restricted license, and most trade-area requirements cannot be fully confirmed.

claims.text: CTE is one of the teacher license areas, with sub-areas such as Agriculture Education, Business, Finance, and Information Technology Education, Family and Consumer Sciences, Marketing Education, and Trade and Industrial Education.
A teacher license generally requires completion of an educator preparation program at the bachelor's (A-Level), master's (M-Level), specialist (S-Level), or doctoral (D-Level) degree level.

Exception for CTE: an applicant with a high school diploma (or equivalent) or an associate's degree (V-Level) may be issued a teaching license in Career and Technical Education, provided the applicant meets all other requirements for the license classification sought.

Each teacher license must be classified as one of the listed types, such as Initial Professional License (LICN-020), Continuing Professional License (LICN-024), Residency License (LICN-019), Limited License (LICN-023), Permit to Teach (LICN-017), Emergency License (LICN-018), or Lifetime License (LICN-027). The qualifications depend on the classification chosen.

Testing for CTE (grades 6-12) listed in the policy table: Family and Consumer Sciences (code 710) requires Praxis 5123 with a score of 151; Marketing Education (730) requires 5561 with 156; Technology Education (820) requires 5053 with 157; Business Education (760) requires 5101 with 154; Computer Science and IT Education (765) requires 5652 with 149.

The testing table covers only five CTE areas. The table notes that more information on CTE licensure is in the CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual, which is not among the passages provided. Other CTE areas listed in LICN-010 §6(f) do not appear in the testing table.

Experience credit for a Class V Career-Technical Trade and Industry Education license: one year of experience credit may be awarded for every year of full-time relevant non-teaching work experience after the individual has completed the required training and work experience to qualify for the provisional license.
Non-teaching work experience counts only if it was at least half-time (20 or more hours per week), completed after age 18, did not include on-the-job training, and was paid and documented.
Initial application requires the items in LICN-004 §1, including educational credentials, disclosures, and any applicable licensure examination documentation, plus the application fee.
Fee for an employing school system to convert a license to CTE on an educator's behalf is $60.
LICN-013 lists a Career and Technical Education – Restricted License as a classification to which add-on teaching areas cannot be added. The passages do not define this license or its requirements.
The passages do not define a Class V license, a CTE provisional license, or the training and work experience needed to qualify for one.
